speechtext:
I know that a number have been passed; one had regard to injuries sustained by those in the service. I shall get a memorandum of them all for my hon. friend.
Public Works, chargeable to capital-Ship channel, river St. Lawrence, $1,019,000.

Last year my hon.
friend the Minister of Marine and Fisheries read to the House an Order in Council which had been recently passed appointing a commission to examine and report on the question of the levels of the waters in. the river St. Lawrence above Montreal and between Montreal and Quebec. The appointment was a very, creditable one, the commission consisting of Professor Haskell, one of the professors of Cornell University, and two well-known Canadians whose ability has never been questioned, Messrs. Stewart and Forneret. For several years, and notably during the last two or three years, there has been some nervousness amongst the shipping interests and people generally as to the lowering of the water of the harbour of Montreal and of the channel between Montreal and Quebec. The lowering of the water level has been assigned to the dredging operations which have taken place for the last fifty years between Montreal and Quebec. The channel, which originally was * only eleven feet, increased in depth as the years rolled by, and to-day the policy of the department, if I mistake not, is to deepen the channel still more to a depth of from thirty to thirty-five feet so as to afford ocean

navigation as far as Montreal inland. Would my hon. friend state to the committee, first, the nature of the dredging operations during the last fiscal year, second, the cost involved in such operations and, third, if any report has been made by that very important commission as to the level of the water being affected by the dredging operations?
The harbour of Montreal, I need not say, is of vital interest to the country. It is no more a local port; it has become the national port of Canada. Looking at the tables contained in the report of the Board
of Trade of Montreal interesting figures:	I find the 1S82.	following 1912.Vessels arrived	614	736Tonnage	
Value of merchandise	554,692	2,403,924exported	$26,503,001 Value of merchandise	$87,679,442imported	50,527,497	148,977,605Customs duties collected	8,395,652	24,555,598
The best year apparently for 4 p.m. export was 1906 when the value of merchandise exported from Montreal reached a total of $89,616,459. I have only quoted the figures to show the importance of the port of Montreal in our commercial life as a nation and the importance of maintaining as deep a channel as possible between Montreal and the ocean, without, of course, affecting materially the water level in the upper portion of the St. Lawrence. Indeed, this question is of the utmost importance and affects the whole transportation problem in Canada.
A question that is also connected with this one is that of insurance rates. I remember that my hon. friend the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Foster) last year made a statement-I forget whether he made it in the House or in answer to a deputation composed of shipping interests -that the Government were studying the question of providing, if possible, cheaper insurance rates for shipping. Yesterday the question was brought up from a different aspect; the question of ocean freight rates was discussed in the House. I refer now especially to the other phase of the question -that of insurance rates. We all know that our shipping interests are deeply affected by the very high insurance rates prevailing against our shippers from the St. Lawrence river. My hon. friend will correct me if I do not state exactly the views which he expressed at that time to the deputation, or it may have been to the House, but if I

mistake not he stated that the intention of the Government was to come to an understanding with our shippers in Canada and to subsidize a Canadian Lloyds. I would like to know from my hon, friend if anything has been done in this connection, or if any decision has been arrived at by the powers that be.

My recollection is much the same as the recollection of my hon. friend (Mr. Lemieux) in reference to the matter. In short, the matter stands in about this way: I stated that the Government was sympathetic with the attempt to lower insurance rates on the St. Lawrence and that negotiations had long been going on with Lloyds with a view to that, but that these were not resulting in any appreciable reduction at that time. Some reductions have been made since that time, I believe, but what I did say at the end was: that it was up to the shipping interests of the St. Lawrence river to show their appreciation of the necessities of the case by forming some association, and undertaking to do their part towards bringing about the necessary relief, in which case, I said, the Government would be disposed, and very sympathetically disposed, to lend an assisting hand. From that time to this I have not received, nor do I think the Government has received, any practical offer in that direction. No practical step has been taken to form a basis for the consideration of the Government, in the way of sympathetic aid.

My recollection of the incident is the same as that of the Minister of Trade and Commerce. I am sure the hon. gentleman would help the shipping community, if, when sitting with the Imperial Commission in England, he should make representations to Lloyds. I wish to express my regret that so many accidents happened on the St. Lawrence river last year. There is no doubt that those accidents, which are not attributable to the route itself, are debited to the route by Lloyds.
They happened upon the route.

There is no question but that the ship channel, splendidly maintained as it is, is not responsible for the accidents. Indeed, there is a belief that the libel upon the St. Lawrence route is only one of the pretexts on the part of Lloyds to mulct the Canadian shippers.
I trust the Minister of Marine will give me information on these several points: Is the Government to continue its policy of deepening the ship channel to 35 feet, and what compensation works are contemplated in order to maintain an even and equal flow of the water in the channel? What portions of the channel have been widened and what curves have been straightened in the past year? For some years, work of great advantage to the shipping interests was done on the St. Lawrence route, commencing under the late Mr. Tarte and continuing under the late Mr. Pre-fontaine, and the Hon. Mr. Brodeur, my immediate predecessor in the department. Last year, when a commission of experts was appointed, my hon. friend from Welland (Mr. German) made some apt remarks on the subject of the conservation of water powers on the St. Lawrence. He said, that the examination of the Upper St. Lawrence by this commission of experts would probably induce the Government to erect compensation works between the Great Lakes and that part of the river above Montreal. The result of that would be, in the first place, to ensure a proper water level, and in the second place, the possible appointment of a commission with the view of developing hydro-electric energy. I am opposed to the proposed development of hydro-electric energy on the St. Lawrence by the Americans. We all know that an unsuccessful attempt was made some years ago to secure at the Long Sault authority from the Canadian Government to develop energy. But, if such works were constructed after having been declared necessary by this commission, the Dominion Government could very well consider the advisability of exploiting the water powers on this great river for the benefit of the Canadian people. I trust that the minister will give some explanation on these matters.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
I agree with all my hon.
friend has said with respect to the importance of the great national port of Montreal. My own desire personally, and as minister, and the desire of my department, is to do everything possible to improve the shipping facilities in the pot -of Montreal and to improve the waterway on which the ocean steamers pass up the river^ to that city.
There is no doubt that, as the business tr* this country increases, as it is doing by leaps and bounds, the business of the city of Montreal as the great port of Canada in the summer months must increase. There-



fore I think the efforts of those who are interested in that port will be taxed to the utmost to provide adequate facilities for the handling of the freight that is bound to come in increasing measure every year to that great national port, which is destined for all time to come to remain the greatest of Canadian ports in the summer season.
My hon. friend has referred to the fact that at 'the last session of Parliament I announced that a commission had been appointed, consisting of Mr. E. E. Haskell, of the School of Engineering of Cornell University, a gentleman who had probably more experience than any other man on this continent in connection with river levels, having had extensive experience with the Missouri, the Mississippi and other rivers, and of two officials of the department, Mr. V. W. Forneret, superintending engineer of the Ship Channel, and Mr. W. J. -Stewart, of the Hydrographic Survey, for the purpose of considering the question of the river levels of the St. Lawrence below Montreal, this work being limited to that.
There was another commission appointed.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
That was by the Public Works Department. The jurisdiction of the Department of Marine and Fisheries over the St. Lawrence river extends only from the city of Montreal down to the sea. The reaches of the river above Montreal are under the control of the Public Works Department.
We had deepened the St. Lawrence channel from fourteen feet to thirty feet, and we had planned to deepen it to thirty-five feet. The -reason for the appointment of that commission was the idett that we could not go on deepening the channel of the St. Lawrence indefinitely without affecting the level of the water in the harbour of Montreal. It was most desirable to have accurate scientific observations taken for the purpose of determining whether there was danger of that, and, if so, to find out what steps should be taken by way of compensating works for the purpose of preventing that lowering from taking place; because it would be a disastrous matter if the result of deepening the channel of the St. Lawrence and allowing larger ships to com-e to Montreal should be a -reduction of the volume of water in that harbour, thus lowering its level, so that in that harbour there would not be the same opportunity for ships of deep draught that

there is at the present time. That commission was appointed and it entered upon its work at the end of last session. When I announced the appointment of that commission last year to the House, I was in hopes of being able to lay its report on the table at this session. Although the commissioners have attended to the work as faithfully as possible, I find that, with the data that was on hand and the observations that they were able to make last year, they cannot make a report that would be satisfactory to them without taking further observations during the coming season of open navigation. Therefore I regret that it will be impossible for roe to lay their report upon the table of the House before another session. From the information I have received from Mr. Stewart and Mr. Forneret, I have no doubt whatever that probably at the opening of the next -session the report will be tabled and the result of the observations of these gentlemen will be made public.
Th-e work of deepening the channel that goes on from time to time is not being proceeded with in any haphazard manner. It has been in charge of gentlemen of high scientific knowledge and experience in work of that character, and the material they have been removing from the channel in different places, they.have been placing in suoh -a way that it serves as a compensating work, backing up the water -and preventing it from running out too rapidly. For some years itha-t has been in the minds of the gentlemen who are charged with the responsible duty of deepening and widening and straightening that channel. From the information I have received, I think I am justified in -saying that nothing so far has been discovered by that commission that would lead the department to abandon for this season the work upon which it has been engaged in deepening that channel to thirty-five feet. It is our intention during the coming season to continue that work.

Has there been any
especial change of late years in the depth of water at Montreal on account of the dredging that has been done in the lower St. Lawrence?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
No. The question of the levels of the waters on the Great Lakes and the St. Lawrence is a very curious one. From observation it has been found that for a period of six or seven years from year to year the water will gradually get lower and lower in the different harbours on the Great

Lakes, and along the St. Lawrence. There appears to be no reason for this. It does not depend upon the rainfall. Then will come a period of the same number of years when the water will gradually rise until after a lapse of about seven years from the time the water was at its lowest it will be as high as it was before. It is a natural phenomenon which men do not at present understand.
Is the water rising or falling now?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: It is rising. There has been no appreciable reduction in the level of the water in the harbour of Montreal. There is such a volume of water pouring down past the city on the Montreal side that the harbour commissioners have taken means to divert a portion of that water to the south side, so as to reduce the current on the Montreal side, which interferes with the handling of ships.

And at the same time
this gives more water on the south side of the harbour.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
Yes, it serves a double purpose. My hon. friend asks me if I will give him information regarding the work that has been done on the ship channel during the last year. That is given in detail at page 104 of the report of the Department of Marine and Fisheries. My hon. friend asked me what amount had been spent on the St. Lawrence channel up to the present time. The report states that the total cost of the dredging and plant up to March 31, 1913, is $15,617,893.11, of which $9,610,259.57 is the cost of dredging, and $6,007,633.54 the expenditure for plant, shops, surveys and work of that description.
The quantity of material removed during that time was 85,160,875 cubic yards. In 1911-12 the expenditure was $588,000. The cost of dredging in 1912-13 was $663,229.74. Then, in the report, commencing at page 104, are given details of the operations of the different dredges employed on the St. Lawrence channel. I do not suppose my hon. friend desires that I should read these details. As to the record of work of last season, I find from a statement I have here that the total quantity of dredged material was 6,929,344 cubic yards. The hon. gentle, man also asked me to tell him where the dredging operations were carried on. No doubt he will be interested to know also the depth of dredging at low water. The places, with the respective depths are: Montreal harbour, 30 feet; Varennes curve, 35 feet; Cap Charles channel, 30 feet; Grondines, 30 652i
feet; St. Anne traverse, 35 feet; Cap a la Roche curve, 30 feet; Point aux Trembles channel, 35 feet; Repentigny channel, 15 feet; Champlain channel, 30 feet; lake St. Peter (No. 3 curve to W. B. curve), 35 feet; North channel, west sands, 35 feet; St. Thomas channel, 30 feet; floating dock approach, 30 feet; floating dock basin, 50 feet. The statement given in the report shows also the number of days each dredge worked during the year, the nominal working days per year, the hours of actual dredging, and the number of cubic yards of material dredged, and the character of material. As I have said, it is not all easy dredging; there is some shale rock and some rock for which a crusher has to be used. Of course, some of it is easy work. One dredge, the J. Israel Tarte, is a suction dredge which throws the spoil through a pipe several thousand feet from the dredge.
What is the cost per cubic yard?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: At page 11 of the Marine Report, my hon. friend, will see that the total number of cubic yards dredged was 6,929,344 at a total cost of $66,229.74, or at the rate of 9-57 cents per cubic yard. This covers merely operating expenses and repairs, but not depreciation or interest. According to the information I have received, and according to my own observation, the dredges are kept in first-class repair.

When the Government is able to dredge at such a low rate as 9 457 cents a yard, how comes it that the Minister of Public Works pays from 20 cents to 50 cents a yard for similar work?
Mr.' HAZEN: I am here only to tell how we are running our own department. But it must be borne in mind that the Government does not need to make a profit, and we do not allow for interest or depreciation, -and I understand that the depreciation on a machine of this character is a very substantial amount every year. These are items that private contractors have to take into consideration.

Does the hon. minister really think that even with the J. Israel Tarte he is doing work at the price suggested by these figures? Why should not he take into consideration the matters that have to be considered by contractors and base his price on that?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
It is hard to calculate that. The Government is not seeking a profit, and all we are trying to do is to keep track

of the cost of our operations. The J. Israel Tarte is a suction dredge and cannot be used everywhere. It has a long pipe running from it, and if that were in rough water it would be broken up. But for this dredge the cost is a good deal less than I have given-something like 4 cents a cubic yard.
That is only the cost of men, fuel and oil?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: It includes wages, fuel, oil, the cost of feeding the men on board, and repairs.

Do you feed the men
too?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Yes, we make a contract with a steward who feeds the men on board tie dredge, I understand they are given excellent food,-certainly there are no complaints-and it costs us, as I recollect, about 14 cents a meal.
But that does not include the cost of the upkeep of the dredge.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: It includes repairs.
Minor repairs.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
No, more than that. Of
course, we do all our own repair work at our shops at Sorel. Not only that, but we are actually building tug-boats, hopper barges and other craft. I understand the shipyard is doing good work now. The men are practically all working on piece work, instead at so much a day, and the results are better for us and the men get more money.
Is there any allowance for interest on construction?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: No.
Is it the intention of the Government to build a marine railway at . Sorel?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
There has been some talk about it, but I am inclined to doubt the necessity of a marine railway there. I think the shipyard at Sorel is getting on very well; the men are well employed and the work well directed. I think there. are over 1,000 hands employed at Sorel at the present time. Of course there is more work at this time of the year, when the dredges are being repaired, but a large number of men are employed right through the whole season. My hon. friend asked me a question with regard to marine insurance rates. Whilst this is a matter coming more especially within the jurisdiction of the Department of Trade and Commerce, still it is

one to which my department feels that it ought to give attention. The department has from time to time made representations to the underwriters and to those who are interested in insurance, pointing out that in recent years very great sums of money have been spent in improving the waterways of the river St. Lawrence and in establishing modern aids to navigation, and urging that these things should be taken into consideration in fixing the rates. The rates are not now nearly as high as they were some years ago, but in the estimation of the ship-owners of this country they are entirely too high. My department has also urged from time to time upon the underwriters-and this was brought very strongly to the attention of Lord Strath-cona one or two years ago-the desirability *f giving better rates to the vessels which come to the ports of the lower provinces in the winter season. There was a clause in these marine policies known as the British North American clause, under which, at a certain date-I think October 1-the rates on vessels coming to any port in British North America went up, and the ports in question were paying higher rates than were being paid in Portland, Boston, and other Atlantic seaports in the United States. We urged this matter as strongly as possible upon the attention of the underwriters, with the result that they changed that clause so far as the port of Halifax was concerned, and Halifax is now getting lower insurance rates. We have been pressing on the underwriters the necessity of making the same provision with regard to St. John. When my deputy minister was in London this year, attending the conference with regard to the safety of life at sea, he took the matter up again, with the result that the underwriters have asked us for certain information which we are having collated in the department. We hope that when this information is submitted to the underwriters, they will see the justice of making the same concessions so far as the rates at St. John and other ports in the Maritime provinces during the winter season are concerned.

My hon. friend knows that there has been a strong movement in recent years on the part of navigators and shipping interests generally to have a new channel on the north side of the St. Lawrence below Quebec.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: That is being attended to.

I would like to know
what operations have taken place there this summer. Does the hon. minister con-

template adding to his flotilla of dredges on the river St.. Lawrence? The other day my hon. friend announced that he would do his best to have the Government steamers built in Canada; what does he propose to do about the new dredges that are to be made a part of the flotilla of dredges on the St. Lawrence?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
A certain amount of new
construction is provided for in these Estimates. The construction of a new selfpropelling hopper barge, capacity 650 cubic yards, of which the estimated cost is $125,000, is provided for. We hope to have that barge constructed at Sorel. Provision is also made for a self-propelling elevator dredge for work below Quebec in the north channel. With the dredges we have at present it would take us five, six or seven years to get that north channel dredged out and ready for use. When that north channel is dredged out, my opinion is that the last impediment to safe navigation up the St. Lawrence to the city of Quebec will be removed. We thought that work should be hastened, so we are asking an appropriation for a new dredge. While my policy and the policy of the department is to have as much work done in Canada as possible, it is the opinion of Mr. Forneret and of the other oflicials that a dredge of the character required for that work cannot be built in Canada. In the first place, it would have to be constructed, I understand, below Montreal, as a dredge of the size required could not pass through the canals. I understand that no firm below Montreal will undertake the construction of such a dredge, and it may be that we will be forced to have it constructed outside of Canada. The department considered the advisability of having it built at Sorel, but, as the dredge will be of a complicated character, we came to the conclusion that it would not be wise to undertake it at Sorel. This, therefore, may be one of the exceptions that will prove the rule with regard to the policy I have laid down.
Mr. LEM'IEUX:	Would my hon. friend
explain why a vessel, connected with the Canadian Pacific railway, I think, which met with an accident in the St. Lawrence river last summer or last fall, was sent to Yew York for repairs, instead of being repaired at Montreal. It was established beyond doubt that the repairs could have been made in the floating dock at Montreal, but for some reason, after temporary repairs were made, the vessel was sent to
New York. It is a great pity that after such an efficient dock has been established at Montreal, our steamship companies do not take advantage of it. Would my hon. friend also give us an explanation for the rather long chapter of accidents which took place last season in the river St. Lawrence?
I was struck with the list of accidents this year and, in order to restore the reputation of the river St. Lawrence, perhaps-it would be quite in order for my hon. friend to tell the House that most of the-accidents are due pot to the river, not h>
the channel, but to the errors and mistakes of some of the pilots and sailing masters.
I think it is only fair that the minister should give tnat explanation to the com mittee.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Answering my hon. friend's first question as to why the Canadian Pacific Railway steamer Lake Manitoba, which got in difficulties in the St. Lawrence, was not repaired at the Vickers dry-dock but was sent to New York, I think the reason was that at the time of the accident the Vickers had not their organization fully completed and did not have the equipment and facilities for making the repairs required. I do not know what other reason there could be, for I would think the Canadian Pacific' railway would naturally prefer to have their vessels repaired at Montreal rather than at New York. With regard to the accidents that occurred on the St. Lawrence last year, that is a question that should be answered with some degree of care and, at a later period in my Estimates I shall make a statement. In every case there has been an investigation by the Wreck Commissioner, and I shall bring down the reports.

Reverting to the first stage of the discussion this afternoon, perhaps it would not be amiss for the * minister to give an authoritative statement with regard to the last phase of the Chicago drainage canal project as affecting the river St. Lawrence. I understand that action has been taken by the United States authorities?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
That is a matter that does not come under my department. At the time the application was made by the Chicago Sanitary Commission for permission to divert 10,000,000 cubic yards a second from Lake Michigan, I took charge of the organization of the opposition to it and, with the assistance of representatives of the Shipping Federation, and of the

Dominion Marine Insurance Company, and engineers of the Public Works Department, prepared the case to be submitted. That was a couple of years ago. The matter was argued before the Secretary of State for War and he refused the permission applied for by the Chicago Sanitary Commission. Since then I have had nothing to do, officially, with the matter.
Has it been referred to the International Joint Commission?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Yes, it *is being considered now by the Waterways Commission, and I think Mr. Stewart, chief of the Hydrographic Survey, was detached from the Hydrographic Survey for a time, being a man of great experience, and placed at the disposal of the Prime Minister in regard to the preparation of matters of this sort. It has been engaging his attention. The matter has not come before me officially since then. If the hon. gentleman wants the information I can. get it from some other department, or perhaps he can. get it when other estimates are taken up.
In making purchases for the department in connection with repairs and work done on the dredging plant, at the shipyards at Sorel and on the channel generally, are tenders called for?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
Yes, of course the hon.
gentleman understands that repairs made at the shipyards are done by our own employees, but tenders are asked for the material. It is all done, as is any other purchasing of the department, through the purchasing agent's branch. If material is wanted at the shipyard at Sorel the superintendent of the shipyard puts in a requisition to Mr. Doutre, the purchasing agent, and Mr. Doutre thereupon calls for tenders for the work, tenders are received and the contract awarded to the lowest tenderer. The same thing occurs with regard to lumber required for use -there. All sorts of materials when bought in large amounts are purchased by tender.

I see a very large
amount has been paid to the Nova Scotia Steel and Coal Company at Quebec.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: That is for coal and is done by tender.

I do not question the
small amounts, but I suppose my hon. friend is right in saying that for all material purchased in large quantities tenders are asked under the supervision of Mr. Doutre?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
That is absolutely correct
and in fact I think everything bought there is bought with the approval of the purchasing department.

The most important
question to my mind that has been discussed by the hon. member for Rouville and the minister is that of insurance of the St. Lawrence. I did not catch just what the minister proposes for the future. The Minister of Trade and Commerce last year rather gave some hope to the shipping people that something definite would be done in regard to that matter during the year. I understand that nothing has been done to relieve the great expense that the shipping people are put to with regard to the insurance of their ships. Has the matter been dropped, or is the Government still endeavouring to better things, and what is their policy for the future?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
The attitude that we have taken has been practically that taken by the Minister of Trade and Commerce. I have discussed these questions with a great many gentlemen interested in shipping, and while the matter, as I said, comes under the Department of Trade and Commerce, still our department, being charged with the administration of the Canada Shipping Act, cannot help having a very deep interest in the subject. I feel it would be my duty and that of my department to make every effort to assist the Trade and Commerce Department in bringing about lower insurance rates. We have done all we can do by making representations to the underwriters, pointing out what Canada has done to improve conditions on our waters. In talking to those gentlemen, when the question of establishing a Canadian Lloyds has come up, I have invariably said that I thought a proposition ought to emanate from the shipping people; that if they would make a proposal I was sure that the matter would receive most careful consideration at the hands of the Government, and that the Government would be willing, as far as they could, to cooperate with them in trying to bring about some arrangement of that sort by which the insurance rates should be reduced. None of the shipping associations or federations have made any such proposal to the Government. They are more familiar with the state of affairs than any official of the department can be, and I think the position we take is the right one, that any proposition ought to come from those who are directly interested in it, as the ship-

ping people are. I said that we would give them every encouragement and every consideration. I suggested that at different times to individual members and those who occupy official positions in the shipping federation, but there has never been any result.
I understand that the minister says that he had a conference with Lloyds in connection with this matter?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Yes.
In these representations, was Halifax differentiated from the St. Lawrence route ?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
I do not think that my hon. friend was in the House when I referred to it. For over two years we had been urging from our department, through Lord Strathcona, upon Lloyds, that the British North America clause in its policies of marine insurance ought to be eliminated in so far as the ports of Halifax and St. John and those of the lower provinces generally were concerned. My hon. friend, of course, knows what I refer to when I speak of the British North America clause?
5 p.m. Mr. MACLEAN: Yes.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: We pointed out as strongly as we were able to do-and in this we had the strong support of Lord Strathcona and of the Canadian Government office-that with the modern aids to navigation which had been established, that clause was not justifiable, if, it ever had been justifiable. We further pointed out that these ports in the lower provinces were quite as safe as Portland or Boston, and yet at a certain time in the year, after the first of October, under the British North America clause, the insurance rates went up automatically as regards ports in the British American possessions and did not go up as regards these American ports.
Is the rate for Boston much lower than that for the Maritime provinces ?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I do not think it is now. As a result of those representations they excepted Halifax from the operations of the British North America clause, but they have not up to the present time excepted St. John.

When does that take
place ?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
I think that it has been operative this winter. We have been urging upon them that they should also deal
in the same way with the port of St. John. When my deputy minister was over in London at the Convention for the Safety of Ships, he interviewed the underwriters on this subject, discussed the matter fully, and pointed out to them the admirable manner in which the bay of Fundy is lighted and protected by fog alarms, lights, and submarine bells, with the result that they have asked to be furnished with additional particulars so that the matter may receive further consideration at their hands.
Would the minister tell me at what time he was advised officially by Lloyds that Halifax was to be excepted from the British North America Act clause? When did that actually come into operation?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: It may have been the preceding year but I had the idea that it was in operation this year.

I am not sure that it
is not.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
My deputy minister will
obtain this information in the department.

But the minister says
that the same rule applies to Halifax as that which applies to the gulf of St. Lawrence.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: What we were told would be done was that the port of Halifax would be exempted from the operation of the British North America Act clause.
So that you do not have to pay the advanced rate of insurance on a ship that is bound from the port of Halifax?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
That is as I understand
it.
That is the way I understand it, but I understood the minister to state that he was trying to get a remedy as far as Halifax and St. John were concerned.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: So we were, and we succeeded in getting the clause removed in so far as Halifax is concerned.
When?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Last year; but it has not been removed as far as St. John is concerned.

It was not enforced
by certain insurance companies last fall in so far as Halifax was concerned. I am

quite well aware that ships have come to Halifax without that additional rate being charged for several years past under the policy of certain insurance companies. I do not know whether all the insurance companies act in the same way.
Does the minister refer to the English Lloyds altogether?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Yes.
I know that some of our vessels insure with one of the largest companies in America and that this company makes no such distinction in regard to rates as that.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
No, I was referring to what is well known as the British North America Act clause in the policies that are issued by the Lloyds in London. 'Most of the transatlantic steamers are insured by the British Lloyds.
Mr. 'SINCLAIR:	I understand the minister to say that last fall the British Lloyds excepted Halifax from the operation of the British North America clause?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Yes.

Just one word more in connection with the betterment of navigation in.the river St. Lawrence. Many things contribute to the reputation, good, bad, or indifferent, of a route of that nature. I remember that my hon. friend appointed a commission a year or two ago to investigate the whole pilotage question. The sittings of the commission were many and the wranglings were also many. But a report was made and my hon. friend, as the head of the department and as the official head of the pilots, had to take some action. I do not know what action he took exactly except that I believe that, generally speaking, he accepted the recommendations made by the commission. But evidently he has not acted upon all the conclusions arrived at by the commissioners because I find that the Board of Trade of Montreal is at the present time making a very strong appeal to the Government, indeed to the Parliament of Canada, in connection with this pilotage question. The board of trade is acting in conjunction with the British Marine "Underwriting interests. With the permission of the committee I will read to it the following article which I found in last night's Herald:

Strong Appeal for Betterment of Pilotage Here-Petition Sent by Council of Board of Trade to Ottawa-Urges Reforms in the Present System-Improvement in Service at Quebec and Montreal is Urged.
A strong appeal has been made to the Government by the Council of the Board of Trade, in the form of a petition which has been sent to the Duke of Connaught, the Senate and the House of Commons regarding the pilotage systems of Quebec and Montreal. It was indicated in this petition that an imperative need of reform existed in this particular department of the marine conduct of the Dominion owing to the numerous accidents which had occurred on the St. Lawrence route, due to the present unsatisfactory condition of the pilotage system.
The petition also made plain its disappointment that the Government had failed to act upon the recommendations which had been made to it previously regarding this matter, which recommendations had been based on the findings of the Royal Commission appointed to investigate the matter.
The petitiqn concludes thus:
That it is urgent that the improvement of the pilotage service below Quebec be effected before the opening of navigation this year so that the British Marine Underwriting interests may be assured that the Dominion Government is doing its part towards securing a reduction in the marine insurance rates on the St. Lawrence route.
Wherefore your petitioners humbly pray for Your Royal Highness in Council to promote legislation embodying the recommendations of the said Royal Commission on Pilotage in the pilotage districts of Montreal and Quebec.
Signed on behalf of the Council of the Montreal Board of Trade, R. J. Dale, president; Geo. Ha drill, secretary.
Montreal, February 14, 1914.
I wish to know what suggestions of the Pilotage Commission have not been accepted by the department; whether the minister has received this memorandum from the Montreal Board of Trade, and, whether he intends to act upon it. It is not surprising that the insurance rates on the St. Lawrence route should be so high, if, in view of the accidents that have taken place, the department does not follow the recommendations made by its own commission. There may be reason, of course, for not accepting all the recommendations, and I trust the minister will let us know what they are. The pilotage system, the dredging, the maintenance of the water levels, the works generally on the river St. Lawrence, combine to make the reputation of that route, and if there toe laches anywhere, the insurance companies and underwriters would be perhaps justified in their judgment as to maintaining the high insurance rates.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
The communication referred to toy my hon. friend has been received toy the department and a reply is

now being prepared. I think the Montreal Board of Trade must be under a misapprehension as to what has taken place.
I understood the minister to state last year, that he intended to adopt the recommendations in the report of the Pilotage Commission.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
I will explain to my hon. friend what has been done. A commission, consisting of three gentlemen representing the ship-owners, and Mr. Lachance, representing the pilots, was appointed. The report was not unanimous on all points. A minority report on some points was submitted by Mr. Lachance, who was at that time president of the Pilots Corporation. There are two pilot organizations on the St. Lawrence: the Montreal pilots, between Montreal and Quebec, and the Quebec pilots, from Quebec down, and they are entirely different bodies. I think I am correct in saying that every recommendation made with respect to the Montreal pilotage district has already been carried out. The commission found things in a pretty satisfactory state in the Montreal district; the recommendations were not of very great importance, and we were able to carry them out by regulations, without the necessity of obtaining further legislation. I am equally correct in saying, I think, that practically every important recommendation that was made by the commission with regard to the Quebec pilotage district, has also been carried into effect, so far as we were able to do so by regulations, before the session of Parliament. I repeat, without any reservation, that I think the essential recommendations made by the Pilotage Commission, with regard to the Quebec district, are in effect at present. There is, however, one recommendation made by the commission which is worthy of careful consideration, viz., the abolition of the pilots' corporation. There is a tradition connected with the corporation which seems to be very much prized by the pilots, and they say: we are willing to surrender into the hands of the Minister of Marine, as the chief pilotage authority, practically all the powers we possess at present, with regard to apprentices, the admission of pilots and so on, but we would like to have the privilege of retaining the corporation. Connected with that is the recommendation of the Pilotage Commission that the system of. paying pilots should be changed. At present, in Quebec, the money earned by the pilots is pooled, and divided equally among those who are on the roll,
each pilot receiving an equal amount during the year. The commission recommended that should be dispensed with, and that the pilots should not be allowed to pool their earnings, but that each should be paid the amount he actually earns himself. The very best of the pilots, the men who earn the most money, are themselves opposed to this, and they point out that under some of the different systems which prevail in the ports of the world, the pilots' earnings are pooled as in Quebec. The pilots seem to feel very strongly on the subject, and I think the matter is worthy of consideration. I am trying to give it the best consideration I can. The argument of the shipping interests, who are opposed to the present system, is, that it gives no opportunity for individual ambition, and that under it the poor pilot earns just as much as the good pilot. On the other hand, the pilots say: those of us who earn the most money are quite willing to divide it with the others; we all do our best, and even if the Government should say that the system of pooling the earnings of the pilots will not be recognized, we still can continue to pool our earnings and to divide them up amongst ourselves if we so wish. The matter will receive careful consideration.
That was the principal recommendation of the private commission which has been acted upon so far. There were two more. One was in regard to the situation of the office in the city of Quebec, which is a minor matter. It was thought that the office ought to be moved to some other part of the city, as where the office is at present there were temptations in the way of pilots. There was another recommendation about purchasing a new boat for the pilots to live on at Father Point. This is a very minor matter, but in the near future we may ask Parliament for an appropriation to buy that boat. Every recommendation has been carried out in good faith by my department up to the present time. Whether we shall abolish the corporation absolutely, or whether we shall let it continue in name out of respect to the feelings of the pilots, is a matter that we are now considering. It is a matter that will have to be dealt with by legislation.
Do we not pension the pilots?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman will
perhaps remember that a good many years ago it was felt that there were far too many pilots, and an agreement was come to with

the Government of that day under which the pilots were to be pensioned off until the number was brought down to seventy-five, at which figure it stands at present. The pilots are contending that the Order in Council does not limit the number of pensions and that they are all entitled to the same extra pension. While there may be some ambiguity in the language of the Order in Council, I think a perusal of all the papers and files would show that the manifest intention of the Government was to limit the number of extra pensions and only continue them until the number of pilots was reduced to seventy-five. In addition to the extra pension there are pensions paid out of the fund which the pilots themselves have.
My hon. friend from Rouville asked me for a statement regarding the disasters on the St. Lawrence river last year. I am now able to give him that statement. The disasters last year were not excessive at all; the losses were not many. On May 30, the Canada of Trieste, 8,816 tons, grounded above St. Augustin. The amount of the damage was not stated.
Is that one of the .river boats?	[DOT]

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
A transatlantic boat. On May 27 the Megantic touched lightly at Point Marie. There was no damage done. On June 20 the Pisa, of Germany, collided with the dock wall at Quebec and was slightly damaged. The damage did not exceed $300. On June 29 the Lake Manitoba, of Liverpool, stranded at the Isle of Orleans. The amount of damage is not stated, but it is considerable. On August
24	the Barcelona, of Germany, stranded below Longue Pointe, but was not damaged. On September 1 the Montreal, of Montreal, collided with the Querida between Beacon-court and Champlain, damage not over $150. On October 17 the Tyr, of Norway, grounded at St. Barnaby's island. There was no apparent damage. On August 14 the Hesperian, of Glasgow, stranded at Varennes and Cap St. Michel and was slightly damaged. On July 28 the Crown of Cordova, of Glasgow, collided with the Lady of Gaspe at Cap de la Madeleine. Considerable damage was done to the Lady of Gaspe. On September 13 the Whacka-tane, of Plymouth, collided with the wharf at Indian Cove and was slightly damaged. On September 24 the Mount Temple, of Liverpool, stranded in Montreal harbour, and was slightly damaged. On September
25	the steamer Germany grounded at

Batiscan, no damage done. The hon. gentleman will see that last year the losses amounted to very little indeed.

How many of these
accidents were due to defective piloting?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I cannot tell from the statement I have, but the hon. gentleman will see that several were collisions, where probably two or more vessels were more or less to blame. Most of them were of such a trifling character that I fancy no investigation was held by the wreck commissioner.

In reference to the
pensions to pilots, the corporation received last year $124,080, which gave to each of the 75 pilots $1,680. Although perhaps this item does not- call for these remarks, I wish to call the attention of my hon. friend to the importance of keeping watch over the expenditure around the harbour of Quebec.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
If my hon. friend refers
to the Harbour Commissioners, I shall have to bring down a Bill a little later on in regard to them, and I will then give ample opportunity for discussion.

I will wait until my
hon. friend brings in that Bill.
Public Works, chargeable to capital-To provide for construction and completion of dredging plant, etc., $666,500.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: We have really been discussing this item with the other one. Is any further explanation required?

I read some months ago
of changes which have been made at the Sorel shipyard. In the report of Mr. Jackson, the superintendent of Sorel shipyards, at page 139 of the report of the department for 1913, he says:
During the fiscal year 1912-13, many improvements have been effected towards placing the Sorel shipyard on a good, sound, commercial basis, and the general condition of things changed and improved all round.
Superfluous men have all been suspended, and the number now working are allocated and arranged in such a way that all are fully employed.
How many men are employed in Sorel at present as compared with say two years ago?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
Practically the whole system has undergone a change. Scarcely a man is working for us now except on piece work. Many years ago a large number of men were getting very low pay, $1.15 and $1.25 a day. The change has resulted in

the men getting better wages and giving better results. At the present time about 1,100 men are employed. Of course this is the busiest season of the year.
Is that a substantial increase over two years ago?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
I do not know. We a're
doing more work there of actual construction in addition to the repairing that was being done two years ago. It is a great disadvantage to have men working for six months and then idle for the other six months of the year. Besides the repair work, we are enedavouring to keep steady work there on scows and barges and things of that sort that are required in Canada.
Complaints were made that several hundred appointees of the old Government were dismissed on the new Administration coming into office. Is that a fact?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I do not think so.
Charges are made that there were wholesale dismissals. Are the appointments made, as formerly was charged, on the recommendation of members?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Appointments are made by the superintendent of the shipyard, Mr. Jackson, and he has positive instructions not to take any man who is not competent to perform the tvork for which he is employed.
I wanted to know if the shipyard is run on business lines or on political lines-whether appointments are made as in other workshops or on recommendation of members of Parliament?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: It is run on business principles, so far as it is possible to run any branch of Government on business principles. Hon. gentlemen opposite know- for they have been in Governments or supported Governments-that it is impossible to keep these services wholly clear of political influences; there is no use in shutting our eyes to that fact. But I think that we are running it on sound lines and are getting good results.
Then it is true that appointments are made on the recommendation of members of Parliament.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
Certainly, I do not make
any appointments myself.
In view of the reference to 'superfluous men,' it would be interesting to know how many men have been employed in 1911, 1912 and 1913.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
I think the same number as now. I have not the figures at hand, but I can get them should hon. gentlemen desire it.
Public Works, chargeable to capital-New ice-breaker for river St. Lawrence, $500,000.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
We had some discussion of this subject the other night. The purpose of this vote is to get a thoroughly up-to-date ice-breaker for work on the St. Lawrence, with the view to preventing floods and to give an earlier season of navigation up to the city of Montreal. There are now two ice-breakers, the Montcalm and the Lady Grey. They are not as powerful or as modern as we desire. They were built to serve the dual purpose of icebreakers in the winter and ship channel work in the summer. But the result has not been satisfactory. They are most expensive boats to use in the summer, on account of their tremendous consumption of coal, and yet as ice-breakers they are not powerful enough to cope with the conditions. We asked for tenders for the proposed new ice-breaker, making it a condition that it must be built in Canada. Tenders were received from a number of firms in the old country, but they did not comply with the conditions. Two firms in Canada	tendered-one the Canadian
Vickers, and the other George P. Davey, of Quebec.	The amounts they named were
very much higher than the department had expected they would be. The tenders have been referred to the technical officers of the department to see if some change cannot be made that will reduce the expense without interfering with the efficiency of the vessel.

Is the hon. minister
aware of a memorial sent by the Quebec Harbour Commissioners	about winter
navigation below Quebec, as the result of a most interesting lecture	by Professor
Barnes, and a recommendation that an icebreaker like the Ermack might be secured by the Canadian Government in order to facilitate winter navigation below Quebec? And if so, has the minister taken any action in the matter?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
We received the memorial, but have not taken action up to the present time. We have demonstrated the possibili-

ties, I think, by sending the Montcalm tp Seven islands, and other points, but we have up to the present taken no action to get a steamer for the service.

I may inform my hon. friend that no later than last month, an ocean vessel left St. Catherines bay, at the mouth of the Saguenay, with full cargo, for Europe-England, I think. The vessel belongs to the Chicoutimi Pulp Company, and carried full cargo of pulp. I met the manager, in Montreal about three weeks ago, and he said: You might inform your colleagues of the House that yesterday we cleared a vessel >Vith full cargo of pulp. It is well known amongst navigators around Quebec that St. Catherines bay is practically free from ice the whole winter, and it is said that navigation could be made possible should any transatlantic line make its terminus there. It would be worth while to study this question. As to the ice-breakers, am I to understand that at present they are at work at Cap Rouge or above Cap Rouge?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: One is at Cap Rouge and the other at Portneuf above Cap Rouge.
The hon. gentleman will remember that last year we had something to say about Sydney. Is any provision being made for ice-breaking in that port?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
I have always remembered the very strong presentation of the case of Sydney made by my hon. friend. We are doing the best we can with the machinery at our command. The Stanley has been at Sydney this year, in fact I think we had word that she was just coming back. Demands have been made for ice-breaking in different places all of which have merit but all of which cannot be dealt with with our present equipment. I think I told my hon. friend from Cape Breton that we hoped soon to have more machinery for this work. When the ferry is put on between Prince Edward Island and the mainland, it will not be necessary, I presume, to keep the ice-breakers in the channel there, and so these vessels will be left free for other work.
I hope we shall then have a boat which will give its entire time to that work. We have had to use the Stanley for different purposes; we send her on a trip to the Magdalen Islands now and then, and under these conditions it is impossible for us to do as much ice-breaking as we would like to do.

With reference to my taking up with the minister the matter of Yar-
mouth harbour being frozen up and occasioning a delay in the Boston boats, I was informed by the department that they had asked for a report from the harbour master at Yarmouth. Has the minister heard anything with reference to the matter ?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: The deputy minister wired the harbour master at Yarmouth asking for a report, but up to the present time no report has been received, or, if it has come to the department, it has not been brought to my attention or to the attention of the deputy minister.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
The question of winter
navigation is, I think, beyond the experimental stage. There is no question about the feasibility with vessels especially built for the service. The only question is whether it will pay commercially to construct vessels that can successfully navigate through the ice in the winter. The icebreaker we have designed, for which tenders have been received and are being considered, is superior to the Ermack and to the latest boat launched for the Russian Government a few months ago, because the naval architect of the department, Mr. Duguid, has consulted with the naval architect of the Russian rflovernment and they agree that the Canadian boat will be really a superior boat. Its dimensions are much the same as those of the Ermack, length 275 feet; breadth, moulded, 55 feet to depth 60 feet; depth, not less than 27 feet, and indicated horse-power eight to ten thousand. My hon. friend quoted the horse-power of the Ermack as ten thousand. The officials say it is not ten thousand and that this will be a more powerful boat than the Ermack when completed.
When will she be completed?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: The tenders received seemed to be very high, and we are trying to make some reduction in the price without impairing the efficiency of the boat.

I have sent in for the
report of a select committee of thirty years ago on the question of -winter navigation on the St. Lawrence. That committee heard evidence from a large number of experienced men showing that even at that time winter navigation was recognized as quite feasible. So this is nothing new, the only question is whether it would pay to invest in the vessels required for such a service. As Prof. Barnes has very well said, Canada has lost a great deal of its trade in the winter by the fact that the moment navigation closes down in Montreal and Quebec, business goes south. Of course, previous to Confederation we had not even St. John and Halifax and the whole business of Montreal and the western country went down to Portland, Boston and other American ports. If we had had winter navigation from Quebec, 75 per cent of that trade could have been kept in Canadian channels.
I listened with a great deal of interest to the statement made by the minister of the work done by the Convention held in London regarding the saving of human life at sea. In glancing through the report of the department I find that in the lifesaving service of Canada there are forty life-saving stations, four in New Brunswick, sixteen in Nova Scotia, five in Prince Edward Island, four in British Columbia, and eleven in Otario. The gulf of St. Lawrence and the province of Quebec are left without a single life-saving station. The large passenger steamers pass up and down that river and gulf, and surely there should be one or more life-saving stations on the Gaspe coast or somewhere on the St. Lawrence.
Mr. HAZEN; It is most extraordinary that there is not a life-saving station on the gulf or the river St. Lawrence. I shall certainly have the matter carefully looked into and perhaps bring the matter up again in the House.

Has the minister in his possession any documentary matter relating to the discontinuance of the British North America clause in the Lloyds insurance policy? If so, I should be glad to see them.
.990

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I shall be very glad to show them to my hon. friend.
We will have occasion to discuss the harbour of Montreal and the harbour of Quebec?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
Yes, there will be Bills referring to them both during the session.
Public Works, chargeable to capital-To provide for the construction of a specially designed steamer to be used exclusively for testing or sweeping the river St. Lawrence ship channel, $100,000.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
I have here the report of Mr. Forneret, superintending engineer of the St. Lawrence ship channel, who reports that the problem of properly sweeping the St. Lawrence river is a difficult one, and that owing to the increasing area to be covered by the sweeping scows it is impossible, with the present equipment, to examine the channel properly in the season of navigation. This boat is to be built at Sorel. The dimensions are 130 feet long by 30 by 15- feet draught.
The other evening there was some criticism on the item for unforeseen expenditures, in relation to Mr. Duchemin, who was employed in the province of Nova Scotia to investigate certain charges of jiolitical partisanship. The hon. gentleman from Pictou made reference to Mr. Duche-min in connection with a case in which a man named Currie was arrested and found guilty, of perjury. The impression left on my mind from what the hon. gentleman from Pictou said was that, in the course of holding an investigation, an official had been found guilty on the evidence of a man* named Currie who. was afterwards found guilty of perjury, and that Mr. Duchemin had appeared as a witness for the defence and had tried to get Currie clear on the ground that the oath had not been administered to him in a legal manner. I showed the letter which I am about to read to the hon. member for Pictou before the House met to-day. Mr. Duchemin has written a letter to the Sydney Record, and in fairness to him and in view of the serious charge laid against him, I think it only fair that I should read that letter to the House'. If the committee will wait for one moment I will read the letter, which appears in the Sydney Record of February 16. It is as follows:
To the Editor of the Record.
Sir,-I wish to refer to a grossly defamatory article purporting to be a despatch from Ottawa which was conspicuously featured on the first page of your issue on Saturday last. It deals

with the case of Mr. John J. McDonald, preventive officer of customs at North Sydney, who was accused of partisanship and subjected to an investigation before me, as commissioner of inquiry, at North Sydney in the autumn of 1912.
Your article also refers to the evidence given at this inquiry by one Ronald Currie, who was afterwards prosecuted for perjury, convicted and sentenced to a term of imprisonment.
You say: ' The evidence against the accused was given by a man named Currie. The evidence was represented as sworn to and the office holder dismissed. An action for perjury was started against Currie, who pleaded innocence and set up as a defence the fact that he had not actually been sworn by Duchemin, because the regular form of administering oaths had not been followed. The chief witness on his behalf was Duchemin. Duchemin gave evidence that the oath had not been properly administered by him at all the investigations.'
Every essential statement in the foregoing extract is untrue. The evidence against the office holder in question was given, not only by Currie, but by five or six other witnesses. (Currie's evidence was not believed by me, and I did not regard the statements of the other witnesses as sufficiently serious to warrant Mr. McDonald's dismissal. This office holder was therefore not dismissed; as stated by you, but was exonerated on, the report which I submitted to the Government, and holds his position up to the present time.
To satisfy you on these points, I give extracts from my report submitted to the Government under date October 15, 1912:
' The evidenec of Ronald Currie was disproved by that of Joseph McPherson and the accused, John J. McDonald, *both of whom swore positively that the story told by Currie was absolutely untrue in every particular. I am satisfied that these two men were stating the facts, and I therefore declined to accept the testimony of Mr. Currie.'
I also give you the concluding paragraph of my report, which exonerated Mr. McDonald, notwithstanding the depositions that were submitted to me against him:
' The only occasion on which it was alleged by any witness that he took a direct part in politics was in the matter of canvassing a voter, Joseph Naves, and the testimony in this regard is so conflicting and unsatisfactory that I do not feel like basing an adverse finding on this evidence, and must find that the charge of partisanship against this official has not been established.*
Your assertion that the chief witness on Mr. Currie's behalf, in the subsequent indictment of this witness for perjury, was myself, is as recklessly false as every other material statement in your arffcle. I was subpoenaed, not by the accused, or on his behalf, but by the Crown, to produce the record showing the false statement that Mr. Currie had made before me as a commissioner.
Your further statement that I gave evidence that the oath had not been properly administered by me at all the investigations is equally false.* My evidence in this connection, given before Judge Finlayson, was as follows: ' In this case, as in a few other cases where a copy of the Bible was not readily available, I caused the witness to hold up his hand and put the usual formula to him.'

This form of administering an oath has been followed by members of the Bar of Nova Scotia for a quarter of a century in swearing affidavits for use in the Supreme Court and the registry of deeds. Mr. D. D. McKenzie, who was present at the investigation as counsel for Mr. McDonald, raised no objection with regard to it. Judge Finlayson, before whom Currie's trial for perjury took place, regarded the oath as binding on the witness. Judge Finlayson's view was upheld by a majority of the Supreme Court of Nova Scotia, and was finally confirmed by the unanimous judgment of the Supreme Court of Canada.
In such a state of facts, you will, I am sure, appreciate the absurdity of your position when you question the binding character of the oath that was put to Mr. Currie in this case.
The concluding part of your article is as grossly and recklessly untrue as the portions of it I have already dealt with. You say: * When a Conservative worker faced a charge of perjury Duchemin appeared in court to swear that the testimony before him leading to a charge against the accused had not been regularly sworn at all.'
I have never yet appeared in court as a wit-* ness for any individual who was accused of perjury. I gave evidence at two trials-in both cases as a Crown witness against the accused persons.
If your statement in this connection, like the other allegations contained in your articles, is not clearly libellous, I do not understand the meaning of the term.
Elsewhere in the article you say that I denied accused office holders the right of counsel. My answer to this is that the investigations held by myself and by my fellow commissioner, Mr. Dane, were the only ones in the history of partisanship inquiries in this province where counsel was admitted to defend accused persons. Counsel was admitted at my investigations in Glace Bay, Sydney, North Sydney and Sydney Mines on different occasions. Mr. F. B. A. Chipman, now law partner of Mr. E. M. Macdonald, of Pictou, defended an office holder in one case in Glace Bay; Mr. W. F. Carroll appeared on behalf of another; Mr. Ronald McVicar, barrister of this city, attended an accused office holder at an investigation taken by me in Sydney. In the McDonald case, above referred to, Mr. D. D. McKenzie appeared as counsel on behalf of Mr. McDonald, as he did also in the case of Dr. Horace Rindress, members of the Board of Harbour Commissioners at North Sydney, and in other cases at Sydney Mines, and he was never on any occasion denied the right to appear on behalf of accused persons, cross-examine witnesses and call witnesses on behalf of the accused and present arguments to the coujrt; in their favour.
As I have said, the Commissioners of Inquiry appointed by the Borden Government were the first officials of the kind in this province to admit counsel to defend accused office holders. This right was denied Conservative office holders by the commissioners appointed by the Laurier Administration after the change of Government in 1896. I do not base this statement on hearsay. My authority is Mr. J. T. Ross, barrister, of Halifax, who was the chief commissioner doing similar work for the Laurier Administration after the change of Government in 1S96, who personally informed me that he had never
allowed counsel to appear at any of his investigations.
This, however, is merely by the way. My main object in furnishing you with this statement of facts is to correct the mass of defamatory misstatements contained in your article of Saturday with reference to the J. J. McDonald and Currie cases.
I would ask you to give this letter a position in your paper as prominent as that occupied by the article whose misstatements it is designed to correct.
H. P. Duchemin.
In view of the very serious character of the charges against Mr. Duchemin made by the hon. member for Pictou, and by other hon. members of the House, I thought it was only fair and right that, side by side with these charges, there should be placed on the pages of ' Hansard ' the statement which Mr. Duchemin has made over hi3 own signature giving his version as to what actually did occur.

I suppose that
my hon. friend from Pictou (Mr. Macdonald) will be afforded an opportunity to reply?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
Most certainly; it makes
no difference what item it is. I thought it only fair and right, that, as Mr. Duchemin is not a member of this House, this statement in regard to the matter should go upon the pages of ' Hansard.'

What Estimates will
be taken up this evening?
With the consent of the House we will take up agriculture.
Agriculture has not been taken up in the House.

I quite appreciate that
but I was suggesting that with the consent of the House we might allow the Minister of Agriculture to go on with his Estimates. If there is any objection we will go on with the Estimates of the Department of Customs.	[DOT]
Mr. A. -K. MACLEAN:	Could Railways
go on?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: That is in the same position as Agriculture.

As I understand it, the
feeling on this side of the House is that the Estimates of the Department of Customs should go on. They have already been taken up and there would be no questim as to the effect upon the rights of hon. members on this side of the House at a later date.

The House in Committee on Bill No. 26 to incorporate the Pacific, Peace River and Athabaska Railway Company-Mr. R. B. Bennett. Mr. Blondin in the Chair.

The House in committee on Bill No. 37, respecting the Ottawa and Ungava Railway Company.-Mr. Chabot. Mr. Blondin in the Chair.
Is this a new proposition?

No, this is an
authority to the Ottawa and Ungava Railway Company to construct, maintain and operate the following additional branch lines:
Eastward, from a point on the main line north of the 49th circle of latitude by the most feasible route and crossing the Ashwapmuchuan, Mistassini, Peribonka, Ber-simis, Outarde, Manicuagan, Pentecote, Ste. Marguerite, Moisie, Romaine and Natashwan rivers, to lake Melville or to a point on the boundary between the province of Quebec and Labrador in the vicinity of St. Lewis Inlet or of St. Charles river.
We struck out all the words in section one after what I have just read, because it clashed with the provisions of the Railway Act and was not considered good legislation. It was substituting other language for their rights in regard to the branch lines. Every company can build six miles of branch lines without any authority; but if they build more, they must ask Parliament for authority, and then we make them state their termini.
Who are the incorporators?
I cannot say unless I look at the original Act. This is an additional power for the company.
At what point does the line start?

It begins at a point on the main line north of the 49th parallel,

running eastward by the most feasible route, and crossing those rivers to the lake or other place that I have mentioned.

I do not wish to delay the passing of this Bill, but I would like to hear the sponsor give an explanation of it. It seems to be quite a large contract. If there is no objection we might perhaps consider the Bill later on.
Is it a renewal?

The incorporation
