I would like (to call the attention of the bon. Minister of Customs (Mr. Reid) to some facts connected with the dismissal of the late sub-collector at Ros-thern, Saskatchewan, and to inquire of him if I can obtain information as to the circumstances under which officials of the Government are dismissed, and what is the practice in that respect. Some time early in 1911 it was decided by the predecessor of the present minister to establish a sub-col-lectorship at Rosthern. The office would have been opened quite early in that year but f-or one fact. There was already a subland agency in Rosthern and Mr. Paterson, the then Minister of Customs, thought it better to appoint the sub-land agent as sub-collector of customs, and as the sub-land agent was at that time receiving a salary of $600 a year, it was proposed to appoint him also as sub-collector of customs at a salary of $300. The sub-land agent was ill, he was unable to open the customs office at Rosthern; this illness continued until midsummer, and eventually Mr. McGregor, who was the sub-land agent, died. In the month of August a new sub-land agent was appointed in the person of Mr. Tobias Unruh, and about the 14th August Mr. Unruh was instructed to open the customs office in Rosthern. I see by the Auditor General's Report that his salary commenced from the 1st September, 1911, and continued at the rate of $300 per year until his dismissal on October 14,1912.
I am informed that after the Dominion elections of 1911, when it was
9 p.m. known that there was to be a change of Government, Mr. Unruh went to the president of the Conservative Association at Rosthern and inquired of him whether he was to be dismissed, and Mr. Unruh was assured that he would not. He gave as a reason for wanting the information that he intended to obtain a building as an office for the sub-land agency, and the sub-collectorship of customs, and being told that he would not be dismissed he moved into the new office. I questioned the minister as to the matter on the 9th of February, and my question and the answer appear in ' Hansard.'
Mr. McCraney :
1. On what grounds was Tobias Unruh dismissed from the position of sub-land agent and collector of customs at Rosthern, Sask* katchewan ?
Mr. J. D. Reid:
1. Tobias Unruh was dismissed from the position of sub-collector of customs at Rosthern, Saskatchewan, because he had never been permanently appointed to the position in which he was temporarily acting from August 4, 1911, and because information was received from Donald Maclean, candidate in the last Dominion election, that he had taken an active part in the last provincial and Dominion elections.
Mr. Unruli was apparently dismissed in October, 1912, and in his place Mr. E. St.. George Hodgson was appointed sub-collector. From the Auditor General's Report it would appear that Mr. Hodgson was-given a -salary at the rate of $300 a year for one month only, and within a month after the dismissal of Mr. Unruh that salary was raised from $300 to $600 a year. The last report of the collector of customs shows the income of the office to be in the neighbourhood of $3,500 per annum., I am informed there was no investigation held into the charges of partisanship which were laid by Mr. Maclean, the defeated Conservative candidate, against Mr. Unruh. I desire to ask the minister, whether when a Conservative member or a defeated Conservative candidate makes an alle-

gation against an official, it is his practice to hold an investigation, and if so, why was not an investigation held in the case of Mr. Unruh. I may be answered that Mr. Unruh was not a permanent appointee to the office, but at the same time Mr. Unruh was a permanent employee of the Interior Department as sub-land agent, and if he were guilty of partisanship in one capacity he would be guilty of partisanship in the other. I submit that whether Mr. Unruh had been a permanent employee of the Customs Department or not, the fact that he was a permanent sub-land agent entitled him to the right to have an investigation. I understand that in some cases where such a charge was made, the officer was asked if he were guilty of active partisanship, and if he admitted it he was admonished not to do it again. I wish the minister to inform the House what the practice is. I am not concerned specially with Mr. Unruh or Mr. Hodgson, but I am concerned to know what office-holders may expect, and whether there is to be a different treatment as between Conservative and Liberal officials who may be guilty of partisanship.

speakeroldname: Hon. J. D. REID (Minister of Customs):
speechtext: Mr. Unruh was appointed on the strength of a letter from Hon. Mr. Paterson in the month of August, 1911, or some time after the Government had dissolved.
Dissolved the House?

Yes. If the hon. member
had been here in 1896 he would remember that the same question was raised, and that there were quite a number of officials who had been appointed after the Conservative Government had dissolved, and their appointments were not recognized, they being summarily dismissed without any charges having been made against them. Mr. Unruh was appointed on the strength of a letter from Mr. Paterson, and he was appointed temporarily, subject to his being iet out at any time the minister wished. In addition to that, charges of political partisanship were made against Mr. Unruh, and the Department of the Interior dismissed him. In dismissing him I felt that he having been appointed after the Government had dissolved, his appointment could not be recognized in the same manner as if he had been appointed previous to the Government having ceased to be in office. The hon. gentleman asked what position I take with reference to dismissals in the

department. With three or four exceptions, I have always had the member for the constituency assume the responsibility of the charge that the official took part in an election. The rule agreed to by both sides of the House was that when a member asserted that an official tcok part in an election, that statement was accepted and the official dismissed. In other cases where charges have been made by others, where the constituency has been represented by an hon. member opposite, we have held an investigation in almost every case. This is one of the exceptions. The official had already been dismissed by the Department of the Interior. From the fact of his having been dismissed as sub-land agent, and charges of political partisanship having been made against him, and the Government having dissolved and gone to the country, I felt justified in making the change that I did in this case.

I want to correct my hon. friend, if I may, as to his statement respecting the practice in 1896. I entirely agree with the principle that a Government defeated at the polls has not a right to appoint a lot of its political friends to office. That was the rule in 1896; I do not object to the rule in 1911. In 1896 a number of King's Counsel and other officials who had been appointed were dismissed. Perhaps the same practice did not prevail in 1911, because there was a good precedent against it. My hon. friend the minister has stated that these appointments were made after dissolution. The appointments which were objectionable were made after the defeat of the Government. The fact that they were made after dissolution was not the reason why they were objectionable. The reason was because the Government of the day had suffered defeat at the hands of the electors, having been found wanting in their confidence. I do not object to the principle to which the hon. minister has referred being enforced in respect to appointments made after the Government has been defeated at the polls. My hon. friend the minister gives a reason, which I must accept, that under these peculiar circumstances Mr. Unruh was not a permanent official; that he had already been dismissed as sub-land agent, and that therefore the minister dismissed him. The minister says that be takes the word of the sitting member, who is a Conservative, or the word of the late Conservative candidate, as the case

may be. The member or candidate assumes the responsibility for the correctness of the facts he alleges. If information is received from any other source, if we put a case before the minister, then he holds an investigation. What does he do if	on the investigation
he finds that there has been a case of political partisanship? Does he dismiss, or does he say: Do not do it again? That is what I want to get at, because I am afraid that the practice of the Government is simply to admonish its own friends and to dismiss its opponents. If we are to have a Civil Service that is to be of any use, there must be equal treatment all around. I would not wish to retain any officer who has been found guilty of political partisanship. I do not know whether Mr. Unruh was guilty of political partisanship in 1911 or not. If he was, he has suffered for it. I notice that Mr. Maclean alleged that he was guilty of political partisanship in the provincial elections of 1912. I do not believe anything of the kind. Mr. Unruh knew at that time at any rate that he was in the employ of the Conservative Government, and I am quite sure that he would not have taken his official life in his hands and done any such thing. He is not well off; he kept store in a small way; he gave up his store in order to take up this position. After this Government came into power, on the assurance of the Conservative Association, he incurred expenditures to fit up an office. He has had to go back to storekeeping and into a different kind of life, as the result of his dismissal. Will the minister tell me what is his practice with regard to Conservative officials who are guilty of political partisanship? Does he admonish them only and leave them in office, or does he dismiss them, as he would dismiss Liberals?

I have never had a case
of that kind before me. I have never had any of the hon. members opposite furnish me with such a case, so it is hard for me to answer the question without having some information as to what the hon. gentleman refers to. I do not think there should be so much complaint as to the dismissals of officials in the West. So far as my memory serves me at the present time, I do not think there have been any dismissals in British Columbia, and in Alberta I think that just one official has been dismissed since we came into power. In Saskatchewan there have been only two: one at Rosthern, and I
think one at Humboldt. The man at Humboldt wTas appointed prior to the dissolution of Parliament; and, if I remember rightly, charges of political partisanship were made against him, and the commissioner who was appointed went to Humboldt and held an investigation, and on his report the man was dismissed. I may be wrong in saying that there have been only these two, but at all events there have not been more than three or four at the most. Therefore, I do not think that the hon. member has much reason to complain in so far as dismissals in his province are concerned. If there are complaints such as are mentioned by the hon. member of any Conservatives having taken part in the elections, if he will make his charges, just as a member on this side would do, we will take action, and then I shall be able to tell just what the result will be on the evidence that is submitted.
Mr. MeCRANEY: I shall be surprised if my hon. friend the minister has not given more consideration to this matter than he has enlightened us with to-night. I fear that what he is doing with Liberal appointees is firing them, and what he is doing with Conservative appointees is telling them not to do it again or leaving them alone. I will give my hon. friend a case. The Rosthern Enterprise is edited by Mr. S. T. Willoughby, who is the secretary of the Conservative Association at Rosthern. The minister will find that the present collector of customs at Rosthern took part in a Conservative meeting at Rosthern. I am going to read such portion of the minutes of that meeting as I think it pertinent to this discussion. It is headed, ' Conservatives seek favours at Ottawa,' and reads as follows:
There was a large attendance at the annual meeting of the Conservative Association of the the town of Rosthern held on Tuesday evening, January 27, in the town hall. After the election of officers Mr. Braden informed the meeting that the association was endeavouring to secure certain things from the Dominion Government. Chief among these was an extension to the experimental farm so that mixed farming and stock raising might be taken up. Mr. Braden was very hopeful from a personal talk with officials that the request would be granted. The association was also working on the proposition to throw open the Duck Lake Indian reserve. But the Indians themselves controlled the situation and Mr. Braden stated the department would not do anything until the consent of the Indians was obtained. There were one or two other very important matters to Rosthern but which it is probably unwise to disclose.
Now, if the minister will follow the report he will see that a speech was made by J. D. Brown in support of Mr. Braden's sugges-

tion, and also by Mr. John Hamm. I will not read these intervening speeches, though they may be very good. Mr. Hodgson, collector of customs, appointed at $600 a year and increased within a month, the sub-land agent, and Major Hodgson, of Rosthern, were all there. They were there in one person, and of him we read:
Mayor Hodgson urged the sending of a strong delegation to Ottawa to press upon the Government the necessity of granting the various matters already mentioned. Mr. Hodgson understood the prospects of success were very favourable, more particularly with two of the requests.
If the minister will glance further down this record he will find the following:
After considerable discussion the following men were chosen as the deputation to Ottawa: President Braden, Vice-President A. P. Siebert, Mayor Hodgson, J. D. Brown and J. A. Sanderson. The deputation includes the mayor of Kosthern, and J. D. Brown, chairman of the Board of Trade. However, it was decided that both of these bodies be requested to ratify the appointments. The deputation is quite a strong one.
Now, I put that report before the minister. The Rosthern Enterprise is a reputable paper. Mr. Willoughby runs it as a non-partisan paper. He is secretary of the Conservative Association, as the minister will see from the list of officers. He was the reporter of this meeting. Now, I put it to the minister, what is he going to do about Mr. Hodgson? I have no doubt that if he were to ask Mr. Hodgson whether he were there or not, Mr. Hodgson would say, yes. It is a matter of public notoriety. Well, is the minister going to say to Mr. Hodgson:
' We have had discussions in regard to this matter in Parliament; you are an intelligent man and ought to have known better, and I am going to dismiss you.' Or is he going to say: ' Don't do it again '?
This was a business meeting?

Of the Conservative
Association.

It was called for the purpose of taking up public matters in connection with Rosthern, and Mr. Hodgson, who is mayor of the town, was called in, no doubt, for the purpose of consulting with them and doing what he could in the interests of the town. Does the hon. gentleman claim that because Mr. Hodgson is mayor of the town he was taking part in politics? Because if that is-

My hon. friend knows better than that. I am not saying that a

man can not be mayor and be a Conservative. All I say is that he cannot be an office-holder and active member of a poli tical association.

This does not say that he was an active member of the association. He was mayor of the town and was called in to this meeting. According to the paper it was a meeting of the Conservatives, but he was there as mayor, called in to discuss public questions. I do not take it from that paper that he is a member of the executive of the Conservative party of Rosthern. If so, he must cease to-
Of course, that is the minister's answer. He will tell Sir. Hodgson: ' Don't do it again.'

He is not taking part in
politics. There is no election on.
Oh, oh.
I do not see that this shows he is taking a part in politics.

I am disappointed in the minister, though I must say I am not very much surprised. If he will look over that report again he will .see that the main business was the election of officers. He says it was for the discussion of public business; but what political party is there that does not discuss public business at its meetings? I know that is the way with the Liberal associations; we are always working for the public.
Some lion. MEMBERS: Oh, ob.

And I am sure the
hon. minister will say the .same for the Conservative party. Had a Liberal been the mayor of Rosthern, he would not have been called in to the meeting. Mr. Hodgson was an easy comer. He is the man who more than any other is responsible for the dismissal of Mr. Unruh. He is an earnest worker and he has got Mr. Unruh's job. He was at the meeting and is appointed a delegate of the Conservative Association to interview my hon. friend in regard to matters in the Rosthern district. He was at the meeting when he was appointed, and he accepts the appointment. But the very thing happens that I expected would happen, the minister now takes the position that partisanship can only take place during an election, and in order to bring himself within the prohibition an office holder must be fool enough to allow himself to be elected member of an executive. I cannot imagine

that my hon. friend could find a stronger case of an intelligent man being guilty of partisanship than the one I have put before him. I do not ask him to take my word for it, the public record is there; and if he asks Mr. Hodgson he will get a confirmation of it. As I say, my interest is not for Mr. Unruh. If he were to ask me to try and get him back, I would tell him the chances were not good, and I would also say:	I would not advise you to go
back into that crowd again. It is not Mr. Unruh or Mr. Hodgson that I am making this discussion about, but I want to know what treatment Mr. Unruh is to get and what treament Mr. Hodgson is to get. If there is to be a difference in the treatment of individuals, we want to know it. If we wish to put matters in our Civil Service, both the inside and the outside service, on a better basis, we must have a definite line to work on, and the same treatment accorded to all. My hon. friend oftens tells us that these are matters of reprisals-that the Liberals did the same thing when they came in in 1896, and the Conservatives are doing the same now. He is not helping the situation by that, but only aggravating it; he is creating a precedent which may Be quoted against him, which I should be sorry to see. All through this country men are being dismissed from the public service who are reported upon by defeated candidates. I do not object to the method, but I say that this treatment by the minister should be fair all round. I would like the minister to give a better statement than he has given.

According to this paper, the Enterprise, a meeting of the Conservative Association was held. The report says:
The following officers were elected: Hon. Pres., Hon. R. L. Borden; Hon. Vice-Pres., Hon. W:	D. Willoughby; Pres., Geo.
Braden; Vice-Pres., A. P. Siebert; Sec.-Treas., S. T. Willoughby. Executive Committee: J. D. Brown, John Hann, J. E. McKenzie, P. V. Reilly, J. A. Sanderson and D. A. Siebert.
The hon. gentleman must admit at once that Mr. Hodgson was not elected a member of that executive. This paper says that after the officers were elected those present at the meeting desired to take up the matter of having something done by the Government for Rosthern. The first thing they did was to call in Mr. Hodgson, the mayor. Who else should they call in? The mayor of the town was the very first man they should send for to discuss public matters in so far as the municipality of Rosthern was concerned.
Are you quite sure they sent for the mayor?

I am only taking the report of the paper which I have before me. It goes on to say:
After a considerable discussion, the following men were chosen as a deputation to Ottawa: President Braden, Vice-Pres. A. P. Siebert, Mayor Hodgson, J. D. Brown and J. A. Sanderson.
The meeting confirmed the appointment of these gentlemen. Mr. Hodgson, according to this paper, was appointed at that meeting to come to Ottawa to see what he could do in the interests of the town of Rosthern. The hon. member objects to Mr. Hodgson's coming here for that purpose.
No.

I hope the people of Rosthern will understand my hon. friend's attitude in this matter. The hon. member is complaining about the dismissals in Saskatchewan and Alberta in so far as the Customs Department is concerned. If the other departments have not dismissed any more officials than I have, I do not think the hon. member has any reason to complain. I have had very many complaints from the West to the effect that we have not dismissed nearly as many as should have been dismissed. There are many men in the customs service in those two provinces who, if the members or candidates had acted upon the information then given to them or representations urged upon them, would have been dismissed. When I tell the hon. member that in Alberta one official was dismissed and in Saskatchewan two, so far as the Customs Department is concerned, I think he has very little reason to complain. This report appearing in the Enterprise is all that the hon. gentleman can submit as evidence of Mr. Hodgson's *taking part in politics since he was appointed, and I think his case is very weak indeed. Mr. Hodgson was sent for and he went to that meeting not for the purpose of taking part in politics, hut, as mayor, simply to do what he could in the interests of the town of Rosthern, and the hon. member is now objecting to Mr. Hodgson's coming to Ottawa in the interests of that town.

I thought better of the minister than that. The minister has tried to fix on me two things: one is that I objected to members of the Conservative Association coming to Ottawa to interview the minister.
The hon. gentleman objected to the mayor's coming here.

Not at all. I have no objection to members of the Conservative Association coming down here; we are always glad to see them. I have no objection to the mayor's coming down here; it was quite a proper thing to do. The minister knows better than to sjiy that I am objecting to Mr. Hodgson's coming here; what I do take objection to is that Mayor Hodgson, as land agent and subcollector of Customs, was at the Conservative meeting and took part. My hon. friend uses his imagination and tells us a story about somebody having sent out for Mayor Hodgson and that Mayor Hodgson, in his innocence, came to the meeting and took part only as mayor. The only people who had a right to appoint Mayor Hodgson to come to Ottawa as mayor was the council. If my hon. friend will look at the report he will see that this Conservative association appoints Hodgson and asks the council to ratify the appointment. I do not object to the council's having ratified the appointment and sending him down, but it shows what the Conservative association is trying to do.
Did the council ratify the appointment P

I do not know whether they did or not; probably he would have come here any way. If the minister desires any more information on the subject, he can get it by communicating with Mr. Hodgson. Mr. Hodgson is a man who will at once tell him what happened; it will not be necessary to ask for a statutory declaration, and the minister may take Mr. Hodgson's word, I am quite sure, as to whether the report is or is not substantially true. Will the minister do that, or does he think it worth while ? If he does that, and if he finds that the report is substantially correct, what is he going to do about it ? Is he going to say what he did to-night: That it does not matter ? Is he going to say to Mr. Hodgson:	You have
violated the principles of this Government; we are not going to allow officials to take any part in political affairs ?

I would like to cite a parallel case to my hon. friend. The committee will remember that in 1909 I came to Ottawa as member-elect from the north riding of Essex. Shortly afterwards the then Minister of Public Works (Mr. Pugsley) visited Windsor. Between the date

of the by-election and the general election, ministers were hovering around; there was a great gathering of the clans in Essex, and promises were made to build docks, wharfs and public buildings. The Minister of Public Works visited Windsor, where there were gathered together a large number of prominent men; amongst others the collector of customs, Dr. J. Smith. The committee knows that Windsor is the sixth largest port in the Dominion of Canada; and that in the year 1910 the revenue from that port was $2,400,000. In one year after the general election the revenue increased to $5,000,000. Mr. Smith is still collector of customs. I have made no recommendation to the department for his dismissal, notwithstanding that he has been guilty of the same offence as that to which my hon. friend alluded. This meeting was held on Saturday, August 27, 1910, between the by-election and the general election which was coming on and from which great results were expected by the Liberal party. Of this meeting, the Weekly Eecord, a loyal supporter of hon. gentlemen opposite, said:
Dr. J. A. Smith, who is one of the most energetic boosters for ' Great Windsor ' that this city possesses, made an excellent address, fortified with facts and figures that commended the attention of Dr. Pugsley. The requirements for a new federal building and a public wharf to come under the observation daily, said Dr. Smith, ' For some years I have felt the need of changes in the post office building and I have asked that the building be extended. I am in receipt of complaints every day from the Windsor populace. Goods are arriving here daily with no dock in the city to unload them at. They must be unloaded at Walkerville. Conditions are certainly had,' he concluded.
The same paper said:
Dr. J. A. Smith, Windsor's collector of customs, was seen by the Record this morning and was asked concerning the good news from Ottawa. ' Yes, indeed, I am highly elated said the doctor. I have been doing missionary work along this line for the past six years and always felt, hopeful we would land the dock. Windsor's great strides commercially demanded recognition.'
I ask my hon. friend if it was any worse for the deputy collector at Bosthern to whom be has alluded, to take the steps he speaks of than for Dr. Smith, collector of the city of Windsor, to address this meeting. I am not saying that either of these gentlemen was guilty of any offence.
Is the hon. gentleman reading from the account of the Liberal Association of Windsor or from a newspaper publication.

I am reading from an
account of a meeting at which Dr. Pugsley was called in to bring glad tidings of great joy to the Liberal party up there.

I do not think I need discuss my bon. friend's point too seriously, because I do not think he is in a very serious mood himself. The Minister of Public Works of that day was there to meet ali the citizens, I have no doubt.

In listening to the report
of this political meeting at Rosthern, callea for the purpose of the election of officers and transaction of other business, I fail lo find any statements that accord with the statement of the minister that Mr. Hodgson was called to that meeting. Did the minister find that in the article, that Mr. Hodgson was called to the meeting?

Reading the article that is
the impression I formed.

When the minister had to add the effort of his own imagination to the plain statement of the article in the newspaper, then it appears to me that the minister is making the best he can of a very bad case. I asked some time'" ago for a return in connection with the dismissal oE the sub-collector of customs at the port of Humboldt. It is not a voluminous return and should have been brought down before this.

That report was completed
to-day and will be ready to hand in tomorrow.	.

That is delightful, especially when we are considering the Customs Estimates to-night. Perhaps next year I may get an opportunity of again discussing that dismissal. The minister says he has been very kind to Saskatchewan. He certainly has not been very kind to Humboldt because the only collector in that constituency, at the port of Humboldt, Mr. James G. Richardson, was dismissed. The minister says he expects he was dismissed for partisanship. I suppose he really thinks that, but if there was an investigation into the conduct of Mr. Richardson I would like to see the evidence taken during that investigation. So far as the election of 1911 is concerned, I know personally that Mr. Richardson, at the commencement of the campaign, came east to visit friends and only returned about noon on the day of the election. Certainly he did not canvass, and how he voted I do not know. I know he .has many relatives and Iriends in the East
whose leanings are Conservative. I am-quite certain that he has voted both ways in elections as he is a man of independent mind; and since he became collector of customs, I have never known him to take an active part in the conduct of an election. My hon. friend will have to give us some other instance if he wants to make a comparison with the case that has been referred to by my hon. friend from Saskatoon. The conduct of the Government since it has come into office, as far as the dismissal of Government servants in western Canada is concerned, is an absolute scandal. When I became a member of this House the first thing that came to my notice was the appointment in Humboldt of a man who was always known as a Conservative in his sympathies. I do not suppose that gentleman ever gave a Liberal vote in his life. He was a son of ex-Premier Norquay, and he was appointed by my hon. friend from Edmonton (Mr. Oliver), as land agent at Humboldt. I am not discussing the Department of the Interior at the present moment, but when the hon. Minister of the Interior (Mr. Roche) brings his Estimates forward we will discuss those Estimates.
Was it not a fact that the hon. gentleman referred to 'by the hon. mem ber for Humboldt was in the service for several years prior to that?

He was in the service; he was not removed from the service at all, and, more than that, he was promoted from a position under the agent and given the appointment of agent at the Humboldt office, a position that he had never occupied under any previous administration. The hon. member for Essex (Mr. Wilcox) tells us that he has not recommended the dismissal of this collector, although this collector, he says, took a prominent part in urging upon the Minister of Public Works of the late Administration that he ought to do certain things for the town of Windsor. I have known of many magnanimous things being done by Conservative members. I could, tell the House of a very magnanimous thing that the hon. member for Selkirk (Mr. Bradbury) did once upon a time. It was generally recognized before the last election that the hon. member for Selkirk was going to have a very hard time in his constituency. He did not have a very large majority and he just managed to get elected. A few months after the election he -was good enough, kind enough, magnanimous enough to recommend the returning officer at his election, appointed by the late Liberal Administration, as Indian agent in his constituency.
Had he made his return at that time?
The return had been made at that time.
Ejoes the hon. gentleman mean to insinuate that the returning officer did anything that was wrong?

No, 'but I did not want the hon. member for Essex to have all the glory on the other side of the House. The hon. member for Essex made quite a hero of himself by his statement that he had not recommended the decapitation of Dr. Smith. I am telling the hon. member for Essex of a ease where a member on his side of the House went him one better, took the returning officer appointed by us and gave him an appointment a few months after the election, and the election was quite close. The hon. member for Essex must not take quite so much credit to himself. In regard to this case of Humboldt, I think the minister ought to have some definite information as to why Mr. Richardson was dismissed. 1 think it is only fair that the minister should give us the information because to-morrow will be too late. If the minister cannot give us that information I suppose that possibly we will have an opportunity later on if his Estimates are not concluded.

I have sent for the return and it may be here in a few minutes. If there is any possibility of getting it for the hon. gentleman this evening I will get it. At all events there will be ample opportunity to discuss the case before my Estimates are passed because I will not ask the committee to pass ail the Estimates. We will leave an item so that we can discuss anything in connection with customs on the item that is left.

In justice to Mr. Hodgson, I do not think the meeting referred to, in so far as he took part in it, was of a political nature because he took part in it in connection with a matter that was then under discussion as mayor of the town. I have been informed that there were other well-known Liberals in Rosthern who attended that meeting. The hon. member for Saskatoon (Mr. McCxaney) knows some of these well-known Liberals.
I understand that Mr. J. D. Brown was at that meeting, and that as a result joint resolutions were passed as coming from the Town Council, the Conservative Association and the Board of Trade. Further than that I have no personal knowledge. In connection with that deputation that

came down to see me, Mr. Hodgson represented the town, and there were some well-known Liberals, such as Mr. Bashford and Mr. J. D. Brown.
My hon. friend does not say for a moment that J. D. Brown is a Liberal. He is a member of the Conservative executive.

I understand that although lie attended this meeting he was always a Liberal. This is the first intimation I have had that he was a Conservative. Up to this date I understand that Mr. Brown was a Liberal.
Mr. Bashford was not at that meeting though.

I do not say that he was, but I isay that they met in connection with questions of interest to the town of Rosthern, and that the deputation with Liberals, such as Mr. Bashford, who had not allied themselves with the Conservative party, came and waited upon me in connection with those matters, thereby showing that the matters that were discussed were not regarded as of a partisan character, but were purely questions concerning the town, in regard to which the Conservative Association, the Town Council, the Board of Trade and Liberals at large joined together.
To assist the corporation.
Exactly, and Mr. Hodgson was there looking after the interests of the town.

I have a very high regard for the opinion of my hon. friend, but when he gets into fiction, uses his imagination and conjures up something to show that Mr. Hodgson was only there for the purpose of expressing himself as mayor, I do not follow him. I venture to say that Mr. Hodgson was one of the first to arrive at the meeting; that is the kind of a man he is, and that is the kind of a Conservative he is. The hon. gentleman puts it up to me that Mr. J. D. Brown was there. Mr. J. D. Brown opposed me in 1911 for all he was worth. In that election I had a majority of 45 in Rosthern. Mr. Brown supported the present Liberal local member for Rosthern, and he had a majority of 30 against him with Mr. Brown's support. Mr. Brown has become a member of the Conservative Association,

and that is the very best thing for the Liberal party that could have happened.
When Mr. Brown opposed the hon. member for Saskatoon, was he not supporting an independent Liberal?
No, not a Liberal at all, but a man who was working hand in hand with the Conservatives.
I do not say that Mr. Brown was at the meeting, but I say that he waited upon me in company with other Liberals.

The Minister of
Customs seems to have had some kind of wireless information from the
10 p.m. Northwest, which suggested to him that once the Conservative Association met, they decided that Mr. Hodgson, who seems to be the poohbah of the Conservatives up there, and ready to fill every available office lying loose, should be sent for. That deduction of the minister is a violent one and has no justification. I think any one who has heard the discussion, and the newspaper clipping read, will feel satisfied that Mr. Hodgson was there from the very start. The minister seems to be developing a fertility of imagination which is startling, and he will have to restrain himself, if he continues looking around in this way for some expedient to answer why he does not dismiss Conservative officials when they engage in politics. But, I specially want to call his attention to a case in which one of these great investigators of his did not dismiss a man. This afternoon, just before six o'clock, when most members had left the House, the Minister of Marine read a long statement from Mr. Duchemin in reply to a certain telegraph despatch that appeared in the Sydney Record, in relation to a debate which took place here last Friday night, in regard to an investigation held into the conduct of a namesake of mine, Mr. Macdonald, of North Sydney. In the course of this investigation a witness named Curry gave evidence for which he was prosecuted for perjury and incarcerated in the penitentiary. I made a statement which appeared in ' Hansard ' in regard to that, and an inaccurate summary of this statement having been telegraphed to the Sydney papers, Mr. Duchemin rushes into print. He tells us in the statement read by the minister this afternoon, that Mr. Macdonald was not dismissed, and as no person here had ever pretended he was dismissed, that statement is of no consequence. Then he asserts that he did not recommend the
dismissal of Macdonald. There is very good reason why he did not recommend the dismissal of Macdonald, and it is, that the very next day after this witness, Curry, had given his testimony, he was arrested fox-perjury and was committed for trial, and the whole basis of the prosecution fell to pieces, and Mr. Duchemin, who claims such great credit for not having recommended the dismissal, after he had seen the spectacle of this star witness on the road to the penitentiary, made up his mind that he Ixad better not report that this official should be dismissed. Then Mr. Duchemin denies, as was stated here, that he was a witness for the defence, but the truth is that if he was not formally called for the defence he was their chief witness because it was on his testimony that the judge granted a reserved case. The truth is that it was on the testimony of Mr. Duchemin that the defendant was able to take his case to the Supreme Court of Nova Scotia, and afterwards to the Supreme Court of Canada, and it was on his testimony that all the argument took place. He really was a witness for the defence, although he happened to be called for the Crown. In this letter which the Minister of Marine read with such gusto this afternoon, when there was nobody present to deal with it, Mr. Duchemin tells us that the form of oath administered by him was the form administered for twenty-five years by every commissioner of the Supreme Court in Nova Sca-tia. As this gentleman has only been in Nova Scotia some twelve or thirteen years, he does not know anything about what happened twenty-five years ago, and if he, as a judge of a court, acting under a solemn Order in Council, appointed by virtue of the provisions of a statute of the Parliament of Canada, is holding a court, is he doing what a commissioner would be doing who is simply taking an affidavit? He was not taking affidavits; he was holding a court, and I want to say that there never has been a court in the province of Nova Scotia, from the most inferior court held by a justice of the peace up to the Supreme Court of Judicature in that province, in which an oath has been administered for the last twenty-five years or fifty years for that matter, except by the witness kissing the Bible. Let us see the way this man did his business. I have here the Eastern Law Reporter, and as an answer to the Minister of Marine I shall read what Mr. Justice Graham tells us in regard to the way Mr. Duchemin did business. Mr. Justice Graham, in a long and able judgment,

holds that Mr. Duchemin did not administer the oath properly, and, so far as he was concerned (and Chief Justice Towns-hend agreed with him) he held that Curry did not commit perjury, because of the method in which Mr. Duchemin administered the oath:
The case states:	The defendant was sworn
by holding up his right hand without being asked whether he had any objection to be sworn in the regular way. This is the evidence given about it by the commissioner himself on the perjury trial, or rather the portion of it in the case:
This great judicial official when he was asked as to whether the evidence was given under oath, starts out giving evidence for the Crown forsooth, by providing a case for the defence, as he really was, answered as follows:
Q. Was the evidence given under oath? A, I think under oath, although some little Question with regard to that has been raised. There was no copy of the Bible used. In a few cases where copy of the Scriptures was not readily available, I called the witness to hold up his right hand and went through the formula with the man. It was done in this case.
This investigator would like the court to know, according to this description, that he usually administered the oath by giving a copy of the Scriptures to the witness, although it is quite clear from his statement he did not carry any copy of the testament around with him, and as a great many of these investigations were held in Conservative committee rooms and such like places where a copy of the Scriptures is not usually found, he did not have the Bible always at hand. In his letter he wants to say that for twenty-five years people have been going around in Nova Scotia administering oaths without having a testament, but lie would like the court to believe that he always wished to have a copy of the Scriptures, and where there was not one available he asked the witness to hold up his right hand. I quote from the evidence:
Q. Tell what was done? A. I called the witness to raise his right hand and I put this formula to him: ' The evidence you will give in this inquiry will be the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth, so help you God.'
Q. And he did he raise his hand? A. He raised his right hand.
By the Court:
Q. I suppose, Mr. Duchemin, you determined yourself the manner in which you would swear him? A. Yes, I did not ask any questions.
Q. You determined yourself the manner in which he would be sworn? A. Yes, as a matter of fact at that time.
Mr. Duchemin was cross-examined by Mr. Maddin and Mr. Maddin was laying

the ground-for his reserved case because he knew that his client had been proven to have committed perjury in order to drive from office, if he could, a gentleman who occupied a position in the Customs Department. Therefore Mr. Maddin said:
You did not ask him whether he would prefer to be sworn on the Bible; whether it was a matter of conscience?
Mr. Duchemin replied:
No, I put no question to him. No option given to him. No choice. No questions put to him.
That is the story of Mr. Duchemin and that is the evidence upon which the counsel for Curry, after his conviction, after his sentence to the penitentiary, asks the Supreme Court of Nova Scotia to hold that that conviction should be quashed. He isuc-ceeded in getting two judges in that court to hold with him. The majority of the court, however, held that as the oath had been administered pro forma, it was an oath upon which perjury would arise, if perjury had been committed. This gentleman in his letter tried to urge certain cases in which he permitted counsel. He says he permitted my hon. friend from North Cape Breton and Victoria (Mr. McKenzie) to appear before him in this and other cases. In my county, when he came to investigate, he frightened the life out of half a dozen poor railway section men who wanted to know whether they could get a lawyer or not. He told them: No, they are not allowed to appear at this investigation. What does he himself say in a letter to the Minister of Marine and Fisheries? In question No. 1 on the Order Paper, in which my hon. friend from Guysborough (Mr. Sinclair) wants information in regard to a letter from Mr. H. P. Duchemin, the following statement appears:
With regard to the excluding of counsel, I may say that I followed this course in accordance with instructions given me by other departments of the Government.
While the gentleman down in Sydney is trying to argue that he was very fair in permitting counsel to appear, he writes to the Minister of Marine and Fisheries, who renews this subject as he did this afternoon, that he excluded counsel because he had been instructed to do so by several departments, in defiance of the law, in defiance of the statute under which lie was appointed, which provides that any person charged with such

ail offence has the right to have counsel act for him. Then he said that commissioners were appointed fifteen years ago and that counsel did not appear before them. The answer to that is that the statute at that time did not provide for this being done. The provisions of the statute under which Mr. Duehemin conducted his investigations were absolutely and entirely ignored by him. The only cases where he permitted counsel to be present were the few cases which he mentioned in his letter. In 75 per cent of the cases he deliberately excluded counsel. What is the secret of the whole thing? I do not believe that my hon. friend the Minister of Marine and Fisheries knew this afternoon that Mr. Curry, who had been adjudged by the Supreme Court of Nova Scotia as having committed perjury in this charge against McDonald, the customs official, after the conviction was confirmed by the Supreme Court of Nova Scotia; after it was confirmed by the Supreme Court of Canada, was allowed out by the hon. Minister of Justice on ticket of leave on suspended sentence. I do not know whether the Minister of Marine and Fisheries, who took advantage this afternoon of the absence of some of us who were interested in the matter to read the document by Mr. Duche-min, knew that this man Curry, who had been adjudged to be a perjurer, had been let out three weeks ago on suspended sentence by the Minister of Justice, after every legal procedure that a Conservative organization in the province of Nova Scotia could resort to had been resorted to. So far as the Curry case is concerned, I leave that as an answer to the Minister of Marine and Fisheries and the letter which he read this afternoon.

This has been universally recognized as a very dull .session, and hon. gentlemen opposite, in their fighting attitude, have changed considerably from last session. They appear to have become iquite conscious of the fact themselves, and for that reason on Friday night they indulge in fireworks in remembrance of their fighting attitude of last year, and as a political force they are much the same as Falstaff's army. I do not propose to argue the McDonald case at any great length. The hon. member for Pictou (Mr. Macdonald) took .some ten or fifteen minutes to make it appear that Mr. Duche-miri, who was making an investigation in Nova Scotia, could not properly administer
an oath, and he cited the judgment of Mr. Justice Graham to the effect that Mr. Duehemin did not properly administer an oath.

That was not it at
all.
The oath must have been properly administered or else there could not have been a charge oi perjury.

You cannot quibble
that way.

The hon. gentleman
from Pictou is a master in quibbling, and he of all others should know a quibble when he sees one. At all events, I cannot see the virtue in his argument, because, if it meant anything at all, it meant that Mr. Duehemin had not properly administered oaths, whereas the whole effect of the case was that perjury had been committed, which meant that the oath had been properly administered. The hon. member for Pictou has referred to the investigation in the McDonald case. The hon. member for North Cape Breton (Mr. McKenzie) was present, so I am advised, as counsel for Mr. McDonald.

I was not present at
all. I came into the investigation after this man was examined.

I accept the word of the hon. gentleman at once. My information was to the contrary. Coming down to rock bottom, we in this House know perfectly well that hon. gentlemen opposite are playing politics when they discuss' the manner in which dismissals have taken place. But the mass of the people in this country may possibly believe that there is something in all this discussion which takes place on Friday evenings in this House, instigated by hon. gentlemen opposite.
There is some credit at all events to be taken by this Administration. They have instituted investigations in the province of Nova Scotia. In a few instances they have Been conducted in my county, and I can say that, unless the evidence was clear and sound, no dismissal took place. I have in my possession very bitter letters from supporters or friends claiming that Mr. Duehemin had not made dismissals upon evidence which had been placed before him, but which he had not deemed sufficient. What happened when hon. gentlemen opposite came into power in 1896?

Were there any investigations in the province of Nova Scotia?
' Some hon. MEMBERS: Oh, oh.

I hear * Oh, oh ' on the other side of the House, and objection oft-repeated to the tu quoque argument. I do not wish for a moment to justify actions of this Administration with what has been done by the previous Administration, but I want to refer to what they did as an evidence of the insincerity of the objections to-night. Taking one department alone in the county of Cumberland, some eight customs officials were dismissed, some of whom had been in the service for many years, and in no instance was there an investigation or a shadow of an investigation. I have moved for a return in respect to the dismissals in Cumberland, and let me refer to it merely so far as it relates to dismissals in the Department of Customs.
The first dismissal was Alexander Wilson, sub-collector of customs at Pugwash. He entered the customs service on the 16th [DOT]of January, 1892. Roughly speaking, he was in the service for a period of four years. Under date of June 18, 1897, he was dismissed for active political partisanship. There were no expenses, as no investigation was held. There is nothing in the official record to show by whom the charges were made. I remember in the House last night or the night before that very serious *objection was taken because the minister could not disclose upon whose recommendation an appointment had been made; but there is absolutely nothing on the record to show why certain dismissals took place, * as the one to which I have just referred. The second was that of Chas. E. Kerr, sub-collector of customs at Wallace, N.S. He entered the customs service December 2, 1884. Under date October 26, 1897, he was dismissed for active political partisanship on charges made by Mr. J. H. Logan, M.P. There were no expenses as no investigation was held. The third case was that of Robert B. Murray, sub-collector of customs, Springhill, N.S. He entered the customs service on July 1, 1893, which means that he was in the service for about four years. Under date September 24, 1897, he was dismissed for political partisanship. There were no expenses as there was no investigation held; and there is nothing on the official file to show by whom the charges were preferred. The fourth was T. R. Lowe, subcollector of customs, Tignish, N.S., who *entered the customs service on January 14, 1888. Under date September 13, 1897, he

was dismissed for active political partisanship. There were no expenses as no investigation was held, and there is nothing on the official file to show by whom the charges were preferred. The fifth was, I. T. Forrest, preventive officer of customs, Amherst Point, N.S. He entered the customs service on October 23, 1886. I do not know what caused our hon. friends opposite to show some delicacy in this dismissal. They did not merely swing the axe and behead this officer, but declared there was no necessity for an officer at this point and so his services were dispensed with on January 7, 1898. The sixth case was John Moffat, sub-collector of Customs, Joggins, N.S.; entered the customs service on May 11, 1864. This mean that he had been thirty-three years in the public service, and I can say truthfully, from knowledge of the family of the man, and from having made inquiries in the district, that no finer type of public servant could be found in the Dominion; a man of an exceedingly high character, a man who bore a splendid reputation iii the district in which he lived, revered and honoured by all who knew him. He was dismissed, after thirty-three years' service, by Order in Council, for active political partisanship. There were no expenses as no investigation was held, and there is nothing on the official files to show by whom the charges were preferred. The seventh case was James Kerr, sub-collector of customs, Port Greville, Nova Scotia, who entered the customs service.on 1st September, 1886, which means that he had served for about eleven years. Under date September 10, 1897, he was dismissed for active political partisanship on charges preferred by Mr. H. J. Logan, M. P. There were no expenses as no investigation was held. The eighth -case was Mark Phinney, preventive officer of customs, West Bay, Nova Scotia; They took a long time to dismiss him, because they found great difficulty in discovering any ground whatever on which to dismiss him, but finally they took his head off. So they dismissed in Cumberland alone, after the elections of 1896, eight sub-collectors of customs-cleaned out the whole box-and-dice of them except a few left for strategic political purposes. There was no investigation and no redress. The correspondence is pitiable in some cases- letters from some of these men who had been in the public service for many years and who were suddenly cut ofi from what they had properly regarded as a life stipend, and without any redress whatever. There is nothing on the record to show that the

Liberal-Conservatives, in spite of this treatment, tried, night after night, to prevent the passage of the Estimates in this House. I say in all sincerity, and I am sure hon. gentlemen opposite who have been supporters of an Administration will agree with me, that it is hard for a public man to make dismissals. Any dismissals for which T have been responsible, I have made with great regret and only under extreme pressure; and I do not know but that I have incurred more the displeasure of my friends for dismissals I have refused to make than I have incurred the displeasure of my opponents for those that I have made. Dismissals have taken place under this Administration, as they have taken place be fore and will continue to take place so long as men are human and officials take part in politics. Why do not hon. gentlemen opposite take their medicine ? They were defeated on September 21,	19li.
Partisanship undoubtedly marked the conduct of a good many of these officials, and they were dismissed. Hon. gentlemen opposite have made their protest, and what more can be said ? In view of the record of the Liberal party in Nova Scotia in the dismissal of officials, I confess, I- am surprised at the-shall I say-audacity of hon. gentlemen opposite in coming back night after night to this question of dismissals under this Administration. I have read here the particulars of eight dismissals in the Customs service alone. I think I could give the names of a hundred in the various departments of the Government in my own constituency. They were dismissed by the dozens, and not a shadow of investigation in any department of the Government from one end of that constituency to the other. Let me give particularly the case of Alexander Fowley, who was car inspector at Springhill junction. He was a Scotchman, a man of infinite experience, an intelligent man who had the knowledge necessary to make him a proper and efficient car inspector. Upon his experience, skill and care depended the lives of thousands of passengers who passed through that place, and thousands and thousands of dollars' worth of property. He was dismissed without investigation, though he was not a partisan, with the result that he found his grave in nine months through worry and practical starvation- and the correspondence will show that in a large degree. And who was appointed to take the place of this efficient officer ? Why, a shoemaker, a man who knows no more about cars or car appli-64
ances than I know about astronomy- and that is not much. Hon. gentlemen opposite may take a certain pleasure in charging department after department under this Government with ruthless dismissals in Nova Scotia, but if they want to pursue that subject, we shall only have to meet them in kind, and the evidence we can bring forward will not be very pleasant for them. I do not say this in any partisan isense, I do not say it in any bitter sense, though I have been speaking earnestly. There will be dismissals made without proper investigation, improperly made-let us admit that lor the sake of the argument, and it is to be expected where so many take place. But let hon. gentlemen opposite remember what took place when they came into power in 1896. Let them play the game fairly, realizing that we are now in much the same position that they were in then. But we are proceeding along nicer line3. Men are getting an opportunity to be heard, and that never took place in 1896. I do not propose to discuss this subject further, except to say that, if hon. gentlemen opposite wish to assume the same attitude with respect to other departments of the Government, as they have assumed with respect to this, I shall deem it necessary to read their record in those other departments as I have done in the case of the Department of Customs.

The hon. member for Cumberland (Mr. Rhodes) prefaced his remarks by intimating that this had been a rather dull session. I think we all observed that the hon. gentleman was somewhat dull himself. I do not know whether that is attributed to the appointment of the hon.. member for Portage la Prairie (Mr.Meighen) as Solicitor General, but if so, I sympathize with him and hope he will recover his former spirit and enjoy the contribution he makes from time to time to the debates of this House. I wi3h to tell him that we are not objecting to the fact that the present Government have instituted investigations into complaints against public officials; what we are objecting is the farcical character of those investigations. It has been shown time and again that, though these investigations were held, officials were dismissed without the slightest foundation of evidence. It would have been a good deal better if this Government had adopted the practice which the hon. gentleman says was adopted by the late Government and dismissed these men upon charges made



on the responsibility of members of this House. The hon. member refers to the dismissals in Cumberland and cited one case of a man dismissed because there was nothing for him to do. In that case the late Government did not appoint a successor, but how far were they behind the enterprise of the present Government? Last night I called the attention of the House to the case of a man who was dismissed from office in my county because there was nothing for him to do. And what does the present Minister of Customs do? He appoints another man, at more than twice the salary paid to the former official -because there was nothing to do. I admit that the late Government has not been as considerate in . respect of its obligations to its supporters as the present Government is, because they, the members of this Government, are bound to make dismissals and bound to make new appointments. If no charge of partisanship can be brought against the official, they dismiss him because there is nothing for him to do, and immediately appoint another man to the same position at more than twice the salary paid to the man dismissed. The hon. member for Cumberland (Mr. Rhodes) has made a record in the matter of dismissals. Take, for instance, the case of the poor unfortunate cripple in the town of Oxford, county of Cumberland, an officer of the Department of Customs, who was dismissed on the recommendation of the hon. member for Cumberland. No investigation was held; the minister simply took the word of the hon. member for Cumberland.
I offered the collector of customs referred to, an investigation, and gave him five weeks' notice before he was dismissed. The offer is still open.

There was a dismissal made in my county without investigation; a subsequent opportunity was given to the poor man to have an investigation, which was ultimately held. Witnesses were examined, and no evidence to prove the charge against him was offered. Was the man reinstated? ' No. Notwithstanding the fact that at the second investigation the commissioner failed to find evidence against him, the dismissal was confirmed. I have no doubt that the poor cripple, Bent, knew very well from what quarter the wind was blowing when the bon. member for Cumberland magnanimously offered him an investigation, which he knew would avail him nothing.

I will go a little further and make the assertion, upon my responsibility as a member of this House, that if Mr. Bent wishes an investigation he shall have an impartial one, and if it be found that he was not a partisan, he shall be restored to office.

I have no doubt that the
hon. member for Cumberland means what he .says, but in the face of the record of the present Government in the matter of dismissals, I think Mr. Bent, crippled through he may be, would prefer to sacrifice the emoluments of his office rather than be subjected to a farcical investigation by the Minister of Customs or his officials. The hon. member for Cumberland got away from the point we were discussing to-night. The hon. member for Pictou (Mr. Macdonald) was not finding fault with the Government in respect of dismissals, but he was finding fault with Mr. Duchemin in respect of an inquiry which he conducted at North Sydney, and, furthermore, he was finding fault with the Minister of Justice in discharging from the penitentiary a man who had sworn away the official life of a gentleman in the town of North Sydney. That is where the shoe pinches. Although the hon. member for Cumberland has no authority to speak for the legal department of the Government on the present occasion, I am sure he would be willing to make a defence if any could be made under the circumstances. We had a case in my county two years ago where a man was convicted of forgery and sentenced to twelve months in jail, and before one month of the sentence had expired he was released upon the order of the Minister of Justice in order that he might enjoy the emoluments of a public office under the Minister of Marine and Fisheries. I say this is the thing that public opinion will cry out against, and this is the thing that we on this side of the House must protest against. If the whole machinery of the law is to be so exercised that, because they happen to be Conservatives, the doors of the penitentiary are opened to persons who have been proved guilty of serious crimes, I say that a serious condition of affairs is arising in the history of this country. The Minister of Justice made no defence for the improper discharge of Landry from jail two years ago, neither is there any defence forthcoming from the discharge of Curry from the penitentiary a few weeks ago. The charge was established, and, as the hon. member for Pictou says, the case was taken

to the higher court at the expense of the Conservative Association of the province of Nova Scotia. Then, every defence and every subterfuge failing, after the highest court in the Dominion of Canada had affirmed Currie's conviction, because the gentlemen interested had the ear of the Minister of Justice, the doors of the penitentiary were opened and Currie was discharged. Of what use is it for the hon. member for Cumberland to talk about fair play for this poor cripple, Bent?. The principles adopted by this Government would justify Mr. Bent or any other official in refusing a farcical investigation and avoiding the treatment which would necessarily follow. Has the hon. minister brought down the information I asked for with respect to the appointment of Michael McNeil as preventive officer at Red Islands?
I have not that information yet, but we can let this item stand, if the hon. gentleman has no objection.

I would suggest that the item we are now discussing be allowed to stand. The next item contains reference to a great many matters which might be open to discussion. I think there would be no objection to the passing of the item with reference to the purchasing of a new revenue cruiser.
Item stand-s.
Progress reported.
